answer:
You can leave on March 31, but giving notice won't end your lease. Your lease runs through July 31, 2026. The lease has no early-exit clause, so you could still owe rent for the months after you leave. What you'd owe depends on which of four options your landlord picks. The most it could be is rent as it comes due through July, minus anything the landlord collects by re-renting the apartment. It could be much less. If you did sign a separate early termination fee agreement, the fee is capped at two months' rent.

You should still give written notice. It has to be delivered by hand or sent by certified mail, and it has to include an address where you can be reached. The last day to do that is March 24, and that date hasn't passed.

Did you sign any separate paper with the lease that mentions an early termination fee or "liquidated damages" (a set amount you agree to pay for leaving early)?

DETAILS

### Does giving notice end my lease?
No. Nothing in the lease or the statute lets a tenant end a fixed-term lease early just by giving notice. The notice only protects your position on the deposit, as the next section explains. Under Fla. Stat. 83.595, when a tenant leaves early, the landlord picks one of four remedies (see below).

### What notice do I have to give before leaving?
- Fla. Stat. 83.49(5) says a tenant who leaves before the lease ends "must give at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached."
- That rule starts "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement." Your lease has no clause on notice before moving out early, so the statute applies.
- Counting back from your March 31 move-out, the last day for the 7-day notice is March 24. That date hasn't passed.
- If you miss it, the landlord is excused from the deposit-claim notice duty in 83.49(3)(a). You don't lose your right to the deposit (83.49(5)).

### How must I send the notice?
Lease section 7 says written notices to the landlord "shall be delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail." Section 8 says the parties have not agreed to e-mail notices. So don't use e-mail or the resident portal for this notice. Include your Tampa address, and keep proof of delivery.

### What could I owe? The landlord's four options (Fla. Stat. 83.595)
Once you've left, the landlord may choose one of these:
1. **End the lease and keep the apartment for itself** (83.595(1)). Your liability for further rent stops.
2. **Re-rent the apartment on your account** (83.595(2)). You owe the gap between your $1,050 rent and what the landlord gets from a new tenant. The landlord must make a "good faith" effort to re-rent. Any rent from a new tenant is deducted.
3. **Do nothing and bill you rent as it comes due** (83.595(3)). That would be $1,050 a month through July 31.
4. **Charge an early termination fee or liquidated damages** (83.595(4)). This applies only if you signed a separate addendum at the time of the lease. The amount can't exceed two months' rent. For a fee, the notice the lease requires can't be more than 60 days.

The statute doesn't say which option the landlord will choose, so I can't give you one number. Your lease contains no early termination fee, so option 4 is open only if a separate addendum exists.

### Other ways out
You told me this is a private complex and the reason is a new job. Nothing you've said points to a repair problem or damage to the unit. The military-orders exit in 83.682 applies only to servicemembers with qualifying orders. If any of those fits your situation, tell me, because it would change the answer.

tool_calls.name: load_skill
tool_calls.result:
Loaded wants_to_leave_early. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the tenant wants to move out before the lease term ends. It rests on 83.595 (the landlord's choice of remedies), 83.49 (the deposit and the 7-day notice before leaving), 83.682 (servicemembers), 83.575 (notice at the end of a lease), and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If part of the reason for leaving is that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required, also load repair_not_made. A way out may run through that skill and 83.56(1).
- Check the other ways out the record points to: military orders (83.682, in this skill), and damage to the unit, such as a fire or a storm. 83.63 may be the relevant section for damage; there is no skill for it, so fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it.
- The statute leaves out some cases. The tool does not decide whether any of them applies; say what the words are and what you would need to know.
  - "This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)(b)). This is about the liquidated damages and early termination fee option below.
  - "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(5)). The lease cannot take away the servicemember option.
  - "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). College housing may be an example.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- Any term on notice before moving out early, next to the 7-day notice below.
- The date the lease term ends, next to the date the tenant plans to move out.
- The monthly rent, next to any early termination amount.
- Where and how the tenant's notice must be sent under the lease.
- Any early termination addendum, and whether roommates who stay on are liable for the whole rent.

### From the tenant

- What date do they plan to move out?
- Does the lease have a fixed end date (for example, a one-year lease), and what date does the term end?
- How much is the monthly rent? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- Why do they want to leave early, in their own words? Is part of the reason that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required?
- Does the lease, or another paper they signed with it, set an early termination fee or liquidated damages for leaving early? Where is that fee written (in a separate paper signed with the lease, only in the lease itself, in the lease and in a separate paper, or they do not know), and what amount does it set?
- Have they given the landlord anything in writing saying they are moving out? How did it reach the landlord (handed to the landlord or the office, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal request or message, a text message, or something else), and what date was it delivered?
- Are they a servicemember (including the National Guard or reserves) with military orders that affect where they live? If so, have they given the landlord a written notice of termination with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer, and what date did the landlord receive it?

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the tenant plans to move out. The 7 days' notice count back from it.
- For a servicemember, whether the termination notice with the orders was given, and the date the landlord received it. The 30 days count from that date.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- The lease and any early termination addendum.
- The written notice of leaving, with proof of certified mail or personal delivery.
- The forwarding address given to the landlord.
- For a servicemember, the orders or the commanding officer's letter sent with the notice.
- Move-out photos and the key return date.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do each of these and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below). A few conditions are outside the tool, such as the military orders themselves; say what the tenant must check.

Lease override to show: 83.49(5) begins "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), so read the lease's term on notice before moving out. The servicemember option cannot be changed by the lease (the exclusion above).

### End the lease as a servicemember with military orders, by written notice with the orders, effective at least 30 days after the landlord receives it (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The tenant is a servicemember: "Any servicemember may terminate his or her rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The tenant can tell you. If they say they are not one, this option is closed.
2. The orders meet one of the criteria the statute lists: "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). This is outside the tool: the tenant checks the military orders against the criteria in 83.682(1) (a permanent change of station of 35 miles or more, a discharge or release from active duty, orders into government quarters, temporary orders of more than 60 days to 35 miles or more away, and the others). See the third open question.

Steps, in order:

1. A written notice of termination to the landlord, with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer: "The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Ask whether the tenant has given it.
2. The termination takes effect at least 30 days after the landlord receives the notice: "at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The program's deadlines show the earliest date, counted from the date the landlord received the notice.

### Leave early and pay the early termination fee or liquidated damages the lease sets, in place of the landlord's other remedies (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4))

All three conditions must be met.

1. The tenant signed a separate addendum agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages when the lease was made: "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). It is met in either way:
   - The fee is written in a separate paper the tenant signed with the lease: "The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant can tell you. If they say the fee is written only in the lease itself, not in a separate paper, the landlord's other remedies in 83.595 apply.
   - Where the fee is written is not known yet. The tenant checks the papers signed with the lease for a separate one agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages.
2. The amount is no more than 2 months' rent: "if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant checks the amount the fee or liquidated damages come to, beside two months' rent.
3. For a fee, the lease asks for no more than 60 days' notice before the early termination: "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before an early termination with search_lease and say what it says. See the second open question.

The step: the notice the lease asks for, given to the landlord: "as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). If the tenant has already given a notice, ask whether it is the one the lease asks for before an early termination, in its time and way, and read that clause. Which remedy the landlord picks is open (the first open question).

### Give the landlord 7 days' written notice before leaving, by certified mail or in person, with an address, so the landlord stays held to the deposit's notice of a claim (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The last day to give that notice has not passed, or the notice already went out by it: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). It is met in either way:
   - The last day has not passed. Only the program's deadlines settle this. If they show it has passed, say so.
   - The notice already given went out by the last day, by certified mail or in person, with an address. Ask the date it reached the landlord, to put beside the last day the program's deadlines show.
2. The lease does not provide otherwise on notice before moving out: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before moving out early with search_lease and say what it says.

The step: the written notice, with the address where the tenant can be reached, delivered to the landlord by certified mail or in person: "which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).

- If the notice went by certified mail or by hand, ask the tenant to check that it gave the address where they can be reached.
- If it went by e-mail, it counts only as 83.505 allows. Ask whether the tenant and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and whether the notice gave the address. Read the lease's clause on notices to the landlord.
- If it went some other way, ask how it reached the landlord, beside the ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation. The program computes no date from a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.

- The tenant's 7 days' written notice before leaving. It counts back from the date the tenant plans to move out, not forward from the notice date. It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise (quoted above).
- The servicemember's earliest termination date. It counts from the date the landlord received the notice, and only when the servicemember notice was given: "written notice of termination to be effective on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)).

## What the statute does not settle

Each of these has no listed readings. For each, say what the tool does not work out, apply the text to what the tenant reports, and pick no answer for the law.

### Which remedy the landlord chooses

83.595 lists what the landlord may do when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, in four subsections: end the tenancy and the tenant's liability; relet for the tenant's account, where the landlord has "a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)); stand by and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee under a separate addendum. The choice is the landlord's. Lay the four beside what the record holds (the addendum, its amount, the monthly rent) so the tenant sees what each would mean. Never say which the landlord will choose, and never give one amount owed.

### The notice period for an early termination fee

83.595(4) refers to an early termination fee where "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The period comes from the lease, and the tool does not compute a date from a period the lease sets.

### Whether the servicemember criteria are met

83.682(1) applies only "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)), and 83.682(2) says the notice "must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Apply the criteria and the documents to what the tenant reports. A criterion the record does not show is not known yet.

### Damage to the unit

If the tenant is leaving because the unit was damaged or destroyed (for example, by fire or a storm), 83.63 may be the relevant section. There is no skill for it. Fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it, and say the tool does not compute anything for it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the planned move-out date, the forwarding address, what the tenant asks for, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that the program computes the 7-day date in 83.49(5), which requires "at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), counted back from the move-out date they gave. The letter is that notice only if it is sent that way and gives their new address.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating what the tenant will owe as one amount. 83.595 lists the landlord's choices.
- Applying 83.595(4)'s fee or liquidated damages without the separate addendum, which the tenant must accept "by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- Applying 83.595(2) without the landlord's "duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)).
- Missing a way out the record points to, such as the landlord's noncompliance (through the repair skill and 83.56(1)), military orders (83.682), or damage to the unit (83.63).
- Counting the 7 days from the notice date instead of back from the move-out date.
- Computing a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.result: 83.595 Choice of remedies upon breach or early termination by tenant. — If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord, or the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit, the landlord may: (1) Treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for his or her own account, thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant; (2) Retake possession of the dwelling unit for the account of the tenant, holding the tenant liable for the difference between the rent stipulated to be paid under the rental agreement and what the landlord is able to recover from a reletting. If the landlord retakes possession, the landlord has a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises, and any rent received by the landlord as a result of the reletting must be deducted from the balance of rent due from the tenant. For purposes of this subsection, the term “good faith in attempting to relet the premises” means that the landlord uses at least the same efforts to relet the premises as were used in the initial rental or at least the same efforts as the landlord uses in attempting to rent other similar rental units but does not require the landlord to give a preference in renting the premises over other vacant dwelling units that the landlord owns or has the responsibility to rent; (3) Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due; or (4) Charge liquidated damages, as provided in the rental agreement, or an early termination fee to the tenant if the landlord and tenant have agreed to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent, and if, in the case of an early termination fee, the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination. This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee. The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement containing a provision in substantially the following form: ☐ I agree, as provided in the rental agreement, to pay $ (an amount that does not exceed 2 months’ rent) as liquidated damages or an early termination fee if I elect to terminate the rental agreement, and the landlord waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession. ☐ I do not agree to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, and I acknowledge that the landlord may seek damages as provided by law. (a) In addition to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, the landlord is entitled to the rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession of the dwelling unit and charges for damages to the dwelling unit. (b) This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 . History. — s. 2, ch. 87-369; s. 4, ch. 88-379; s. 448, ch. 95-147; s. 2, ch. 2008-131.

tool_calls.result: 83.49 Deposit money or advance rent; duty of landlord and tenant. — (1) Whenever money is deposited or advanced by a tenant on a rental agreement as security for performance of the rental agreement or as advance rent for other than the next immediate rental period, the landlord or the landlord’s agent shall either: (a) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate non-interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; (b) Hold the total amount of such money in a separate interest-bearing account in a Florida financial institution for the benefit of the tenant or tenants, in which case the tenant shall receive and collect interest in an amount of at least 75 percent of the annualized average interest rate payable on such account or interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest, whichever the landlord elects. The landlord shall not commingle such moneys with any other funds of the landlord or hypothecate, pledge, or in any other way make use of such moneys until such moneys are actually due the landlord; or (c) Post a surety bond, executed by the landlord as principal and a surety company authorized and licensed to do business in the state as surety, with the clerk of the circuit court in the county in which the dwelling unit is located in the total amount of the security deposits and advance rent he or she holds on behalf of the tenants or $50,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of the provisions of this section. In addition to posting the surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest at the rate of 5 percent per year, simple interest. A landlord, or the landlord’s agent, engaged in the renting of dwelling units in five or more counties, who holds deposit moneys or advance rent and who is otherwise subject to the provisions of this section, may, in lieu of posting a surety bond in each county, elect to post a surety bond in the form and manner provided in this paragraph with the office of the Secretary of State. The bond shall be in the total amount of the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of tenants or in the amount of $250,000, whichever is less. The bond shall be conditioned upon the faithful compliance of the landlord with the provisions of this section and shall run to the Governor for the benefit of any tenant injured by the landlord’s violation of this section. In addition to posting a surety bond, the landlord shall pay to the tenant interest on the security deposit or advance rent held on behalf of that tenant at the rate of 5 percent per year simple interest. (2) The landlord shall, in the lease agreement or within 30 days after receipt of advance rent or a security deposit, give written notice to the tenant which includes disclosure of the advance rent or security deposit. Subsequent to providing such written notice, if the landlord changes the manner or location in which he or she is holding the advance rent or security deposit, he or she must notify the tenant within 30 days after the change as provided in paragraphs (a)-(d). The landlord is not required to give new or additional notice solely because the depository has merged with another financial institution, changed its name, or transferred ownership to a different financial institution. This subsection does not apply to any landlord who rents fewer than five individual dwelling units. Failure to give this notice is not a defense to the payment of rent when due. The written notice must: (a) Be given in person or delivered by mail or e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 to the tenant. (b) State the name and address of the depository where the advance rent or security deposit is being held or state that the landlord has posted a surety bond as provided by law. (c) State whether the tenant is entitled to interest on the deposit. (d) Contain the following disclosure: YOUR RENTAL AGREEMENT REQUIRES PAYMENT OF CERTAIN DEPOSITS. THE LANDLORD MAY TRANSFER ADVANCE RENTS TO THE LANDLORD’S ACCOUNT AS THEY ARE DUE AND WITHOUT NOTICE. WHEN YOU MOVE OUT, YOU MUST GIVE THE LANDLORD YOUR NEW ADDRESS SO THAT THE LANDLORD CAN SEND YOU NOTICES REGARDING YOUR DEPOSIT. THE LANDLORD MUST PROVIDE YOU WRITTEN NOTICE IN PERSON, BY MAIL, OR BY E-MAIL IN ACCORDANCE WITH SECTION 83.505 , FLORIDA STATUTES, WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT, OF THE LANDLORD’S INTENT TO IMPOSE A CLAIM AGAINST THE DEPOSIT. IF YOU DO NOT REPLY TO THE LANDLORD STATING YOUR OBJECTION TO THE CLAIM WITHIN 15 DAYS AFTER RECEIPT OF THE LANDLORD’S WRITTEN NOTICE, THE LANDLORD WILL COLLECT THE CLAIM AND MUST MAIL YOU THE REMAINING DEPOSIT, IF ANY. IF THE LANDLORD FAILS TO TIMELY PROVIDE YOU NOTICE, THE LANDLORD MUST RETURN THE DEPOSIT BUT MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT AGAINST YOU FOR DAMAGES. IF YOU FAIL TO TIMELY OBJECT TO A CLAIM, THE LANDLORD MAY COLLECT FROM THE DEPOSIT, BUT YOU MAY LATER FILE A LAWSUIT CLAIMING A REFUND. YOU SHOULD ATTEMPT TO INFORMALLY RESOLVE ANY DISPUTE BEFORE FILING A LAWSUIT. GENERALLY, THE PARTY IN WHOSE FAVOR A JUDGMENT IS RENDERED WILL BE AWARDED COSTS AND ATTORNEY FEES PAYABLE BY THE LOSING PARTY. THIS DISCLOSURE IS BASIC. PLEASE REFER TO PART II OF CHAPTER 83, FLORIDA STATUTES, TO DETERMINE YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS AND OBLIGATIONS. (3) The landlord or the landlord’s agent may disburse advance rents from the deposit account to the landlord’s benefit when the advance rental period commences and without notice to the tenant. For all other deposits: (a) Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement, if the landlord does not intend to impose a claim on the security deposit, the landlord must return the security deposit, together with interest if otherwise required, within 15 days after the termination of the rental agreement. If the landlord intends to impose a claim on the deposit, the landlord must, within 30 days after the termination of the rental agreement, provide the tenant written notice by certified mail to the tenant’s last known mailing address or by e-mail in accordance with s. 83.505 of his or her intention to impose a claim on the deposit and the reason for imposing the claim. The written notice must contain a statement in substantially the following form: This is a notice of my intention to impose a claim for damages in the amount of upon your security deposit, due to . It is sent to you as required by s. 83.49 (3), Florida Statutes. You are hereby notified that you must object in writing to this deduction from your security deposit within 15 days after the time you receive this notice or I will be authorized to deduct my claim from your security deposit. Your objection must be sent to (landlord’s address) . If the landlord fails to give the required written notice within the 30-day period, he or she forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit and may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant. (b) Unless the tenant objects to the imposition of the landlord’s claim or the amount thereof within 15 days after receipt of the landlord’s notice of intention to impose a claim, the landlord may then deduct the amount of his or her claim and shall remit the balance of the deposit to the tenant within 30 days after the date of the notice of intention to impose a claim for damages. The failure of the tenant to make a timely objection does not waive any rights of the tenant to seek damages in a separate action. (c) If either party institutes an action in a court of competent jurisdiction to adjudicate the party’s right to the security deposit, the prevailing party is entitled to receive his or her court costs plus a reasonable fee for his or her attorney. The court shall advance the cause on the calendar. (d) Compliance with this section by an individual or business entity authorized to conduct business in this state, including Florida-licensed real estate brokers and sales associates, constitutes compliance with all other relevant Florida Statutes pertaining to security deposits held pursuant to a rental agreement or other landlord-tenant relationship. Enforcement personnel shall look solely to this section to determine compliance. This section prevails over any conflicting provisions in chapter 475 and in other sections of the Florida Statutes, and shall operate to permit licensed real estate brokers to disburse security deposits and deposit money without having to comply with the notice and settlement procedures contained in s. 475.25 (1)(d). (4) This section does not apply to transient rentals by hotels or motels as defined in chapter 509 or in those instances in which the amount of rent or deposit, or both, is regulated by law or by rules or regulations of a public body, including public housing authorities and federally administered or regulated housing programs including s. 202, s. 221(d)(3) and (4), s. 236, or s. 8 of the National Housing Act, as amended, other than for rent stabilization. With the exception of subsections (3), (5), and (6), this section is not applicable to housing authorities or public housing agencies created pursuant to chapter 421 or other statutes. (5) Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement, any tenant who vacates or abandons the premises before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement, or any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year, must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached. Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it. answer:
You probably don't owe the $3,000 as a flat fee, because it is more than the law allows. That doesn't mean leaving costs nothing. Florida lets a landlord charge an early termination fee only if it is no more than 2 months' rent. Your rent is $1,050, so the cap is $2,100, and your addendum says $3,000. Without a valid fee, your landlord can use its other options for a tenant who leaves early. One option is to hold you to the rent as it comes due through July 31, 2026. Another is to try in good faith to re-rent the apartment and charge you only the shortfall. I can't say which option your landlord would pick or what you would owe.

One point is unsettled: whether the addendum's promise to waive extra rent still holds when the fee itself is over the cap. The statute doesn't say. You could argue that the whole addendum fails. Your landlord could argue that only the amount above the cap fails.

Your lease also requires 30 days' written notice of early termination. For an April 30 move-out, that notice is due by March 31, 2026, which has not passed.

Do you plan to deliver the notice by hand to the office or by certified mail?

DETAILS

### Is the $3,000 allowed under the early termination fee rule?

- Your addendum is a separate signed paper. You checked the box agreeing to pay "$3,000.00 as liquidated damages or an early termination fee." That meets the "separate addendum" requirement in Fla. Stat. 83.595(4).
- The same subsection allows the fee only "if the amount does not exceed 2 months' rent." Two months of your $1,050 rent is $2,100, so $3,000 is over the cap.
- The statute's model addendum wording also says the amount is "an amount that does not exceed 2 months' rent." Your addendum doesn't meet that.
- Your landlord can't use the fee remedy in 83.595(4) as written. The statute doesn't say what happens to a fee that is too high. It could be void entirely, or enforceable only up to $2,100. I can't settle that for you.

### What else could your landlord do if the fee doesn't apply?

Under Fla. Stat. 83.595, when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, the landlord may do one of four things:
1. Treat the lease as ended and retake the unit "thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant" (83.595(1)).
2. Retake the unit for your account and hold you liable for the difference between your rent and what re-renting brings in. The landlord must use good faith to re-rent it (83.595(2)).
3. "Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due" (83.595(3)).
4. Charge the fee, only if the conditions in 83.595(4) are met.

The choice is your landlord's. Your lease runs through July 31, 2026, so options 2 and 3 could involve rent after April 30. I won't give a single amount, because it depends on which option your landlord picks and on whether the apartment is re-rented.

### What does your lease require for notice?

- Clause 11 says you may end the lease early "by giving Landlord 30 days' written notice, delivered as clause 7 says, and paying the amount Tenant agreed to in Addendum A."
- Clause 7 says written notices go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail."
- For an April 30 move-out, the 30-day notice date is March 31, 2026. It has not passed.
- A 30-day notice period is within the 60-day limit in 83.595(4) for fee notice.
- E-mail, a text, or a portal message would not follow the lease. Clause 8 says you and your landlord have not agreed to e-mail notices.

### Is there a separate 7-day notice?

- Fla. Stat. 83.49(5) asks for "at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached." This protects your rights around the security deposit.
- Counted back from April 30, that date is April 23, 2026. It has not passed.
- If you send the clause 11 notice by hand or certified mail, with your new address, it can cover both requirements.
- You have given no notice yet.

Loaded wants_to_leave_early. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the tenant wants to move out before the lease term ends. It rests on 83.595 (the landlord's choice of remedies), 83.49 (the deposit and the 7-day notice before leaving), 83.682 (servicemembers), 83.575 (notice at the end of a lease), and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If part of the reason for leaving is that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required, also load repair_not_made. A way out may run through that skill and 83.56(1).
- Check the other ways out the record points to: military orders (83.682, in this skill), and damage to the unit, such as a fire or a storm. 83.63 may be the relevant section for damage; there is no skill for it, so fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it.
- The statute leaves out some cases. The tool does not decide whether any of them applies; say what the words are and what you would need to know.
  - "This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)(b)). This is about the liquidated damages and early termination fee option below.
  - "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(5)). The lease cannot take away the servicemember option.
  - "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). College housing may be an example.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- Any term on notice before moving out early, next to the 7-day notice below.
- The date the lease term ends, next to the date the tenant plans to move out.
- The monthly rent, next to any early termination amount.
- Where and how the tenant's notice must be sent under the lease.
- Any early termination addendum, and whether roommates who stay on are liable for the whole rent.

### From the tenant

- What date do they plan to move out?
- Does the lease have a fixed end date (for example, a one-year lease), and what date does the term end?
- How much is the monthly rent? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- Why do they want to leave early, in their own words? Is part of the reason that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required?
- Does the lease, or another paper they signed with it, set an early termination fee or liquidated damages for leaving early? Where is that fee written (in a separate paper signed with the lease, only in the lease itself, in the lease and in a separate paper, or they do not know), and what amount does it set?
- Have they given the landlord anything in writing saying they are moving out? How did it reach the landlord (handed to the landlord or the office, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal request or message, a text message, or something else), and what date was it delivered?
- Are they a servicemember (including the National Guard or reserves) with military orders that affect where they live? If so, have they given the landlord a written notice of termination with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer, and what date did the landlord receive it?

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the tenant plans to move out. The 7 days' notice count back from it.
- For a servicemember, whether the termination notice with the orders was given, and the date the landlord received it. The 30 days count from that date.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- The lease and any early termination addendum.
- The written notice of leaving, with proof of certified mail or personal delivery.
- The forwarding address given to the landlord.
- For a servicemember, the orders or the commanding officer's letter sent with the notice.
- Move-out photos and the key return date.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do each of these and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below). A few conditions are outside the tool, such as the military orders themselves; say what the tenant must check.

Lease override to show: 83.49(5) begins "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), so read the lease's term on notice before moving out. The servicemember option cannot be changed by the lease (the exclusion above).

### End the lease as a servicemember with military orders, by written notice with the orders, effective at least 30 days after the landlord receives it (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The tenant is a servicemember: "Any servicemember may terminate his or her rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The tenant can tell you. If they say they are not one, this option is closed.
2. The orders meet one of the criteria the statute lists: "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). This is outside the tool: the tenant checks the military orders against the criteria in 83.682(1) (a permanent change of station of 35 miles or more, a discharge or release from active duty, orders into government quarters, temporary orders of more than 60 days to 35 miles or more away, and the others). See the third open question.

Steps, in order:

1. A written notice of termination to the landlord, with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer: "The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Ask whether the tenant has given it.
2. The termination takes effect at least 30 days after the landlord receives the notice: "at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The program's deadlines show the earliest date, counted from the date the landlord received the notice.

### Leave early and pay the early termination fee or liquidated damages the lease sets, in place of the landlord's other remedies (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4))

All three conditions must be met.

1. The tenant signed a separate addendum agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages when the lease was made: "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). It is met in either way:
   - The fee is written in a separate paper the tenant signed with the lease: "The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant can tell you. If they say the fee is written only in the lease itself, not in a separate paper, the landlord's other remedies in 83.595 apply.
   - Where the fee is written is not known yet. The tenant checks the papers signed with the lease for a separate one agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages.
2. The amount is no more than 2 months' rent: "if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant checks the amount the fee or liquidated damages come to, beside two months' rent.
3. For a fee, the lease asks for no more than 60 days' notice before the early termination: "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before an early termination with search_lease and say what it says. See the second open question.

The step: the notice the lease asks for, given to the landlord: "as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). If the tenant has already given a notice, ask whether it is the one the lease asks for before an early termination, in its time and way, and read that clause. Which remedy the landlord picks is open (the first open question).

### Give the landlord 7 days' written notice before leaving, by certified mail or in person, with an address, so the landlord stays held to the deposit's notice of a claim (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The last day to give that notice has not passed, or the notice already went out by it: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). It is met in either way:
   - The last day has not passed. Only the program's deadlines settle this. If they show it has passed, say so.
   - The notice already given went out by the last day, by certified mail or in person, with an address. Ask the date it reached the landlord, to put beside the last day the program's deadlines show.
2. The lease does not provide otherwise on notice before moving out: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before moving out early with search_lease and say what it says.

The step: the written notice, with the address where the tenant can be reached, delivered to the landlord by certified mail or in person: "which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).

- If the notice went by certified mail or by hand, ask the tenant to check that it gave the address where they can be reached.
- If it went by e-mail, it counts only as 83.505 allows. Ask whether the tenant and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and whether the notice gave the address. Read the lease's clause on notices to the landlord.
- If it went some other way, ask how it reached the landlord, beside the ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation. The program computes no date from a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.

- The tenant's 7 days' written notice before leaving. It counts back from the date the tenant plans to move out, not forward from the notice date. It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise (quoted above).
- The servicemember's earliest termination date. It counts from the date the landlord received the notice, and only when the servicemember notice was given: "written notice of termination to be effective on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)).

## What the statute does not settle

Each of these has no listed readings. For each, say what the tool does not work out, apply the text to what the tenant reports, and pick no answer for the law.

### Which remedy the landlord chooses

83.595 lists what the landlord may do when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, in four subsections: end the tenancy and the tenant's liability; relet for the tenant's account, where the landlord has "a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)); stand by and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee under a separate addendum. The choice is the landlord's. Lay the four beside what the record holds (the addendum, its amount, the monthly rent) so the tenant sees what each would mean. Never say which the landlord will choose, and never give one amount owed.

### The notice period for an early termination fee

83.595(4) refers to an early termination fee where "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The period comes from the lease, and the tool does not compute a date from a period the lease sets.

### Whether the servicemember criteria are met

83.682(1) applies only "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)), and 83.682(2) says the notice "must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Apply the criteria and the documents to what the tenant reports. A criterion the record does not show is not known yet.

### Damage to the unit

If the tenant is leaving because the unit was damaged or destroyed (for example, by fire or a storm), 83.63 may be the relevant section. There is no skill for it. Fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it, and say the tool does not compute anything for it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the planned move-out date, the forwarding address, what the tenant asks for, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that the program computes the 7-day date in 83.49(5), which requires "at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), counted back from the move-out date they gave. The letter is that notice only if it is sent that way and gives their new address.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating what the tenant will owe as one amount. 83.595 lists the landlord's choices.
- Applying 83.595(4)'s fee or liquidated damages without the separate addendum, which the tenant must accept "by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- Applying 83.595(2) without the landlord's "duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)).
- Missing a way out the record points to, such as the landlord's noncompliance (through the repair skill and 83.56(1)), military orders (83.682), or damage to the unit (83.63).
- Counting the 7 days from the notice date instead of back from the move-out date.
- Computing a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.
- Computing any date yourself.

answer:
**Not yet, and part of the answer is not settled.** The law lets a tenant end a lease over a repair the landlord won't make. First, though, you have to give a specific written notice, and your portal requests don't count as that notice. Two other points are open. One is whether the leak counts as serious enough. The other is whether paying April rent while you knew about the leak costs you this right.

If you skip the notice and just leave, the landlord can treat you as breaking the lease. Your landlord would then choose how to handle it, which could include holding you to the rent through July 31, 2026.

Have you given your landlord any other written notice about the leak, handed to the office or sent by certified mail? If so, what did it say, and on what date did it arrive?

DETAILS

### Is a leaking roof your landlord's job to fix?
- Yes, as far as the statute goes. Section 83.51(1)(b) says that where no local code applies, the landlord must "maintain the roofs, windows, doors, floors, steps, porches, exterior walls, foundations, and all other structural components in good repair."
- Section 83.51(1)(a) says the landlord must follow "applicable building, housing, and health codes." Whether a Gainesville or Alachua County code covers this leak is outside this tool. The code office can tell you and can inspect.
- You told me rain is coming through the roof and you did nothing to cause it. Under section 83.51(4), the landlord is not responsible only for problems the tenant or the tenant's guests caused. That exception doesn't apply to what you described.
- Your building has many units, so section 83.51(1) can't be changed by a written agreement the way it can for a house or duplex. Your lease has no clause that shifts roof repairs to you.

### Did your portal requests count as notice that you'll end the lease?
- No. Section 83.56(1) requires "written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement by reason thereof."
- Your two requests (March 21 and April 2) asked for a repair. Neither said you would end the lease.
- Section 83.56(4) names the allowed ways to deliver this notice: mailing it, delivering a true copy, or e-mailing it under section 83.505. A portal message is not on that list.
- Your lease, section 7, says notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail." Section 8 says you and the landlord have not agreed to e-mail notices.
- A notice that fits the statute and your lease would name the leak, say you will end the lease if it isn't fixed, and be handed to the office or sent by certified mail.
- The landlord then has 7 days after the notice is delivered to fix the leak. I can only count that deadline once you confirm the date it was delivered. I can't tell you yet whether it would pass before May 15.

### Is the leak serious enough?
- Whether the landlord "materially" failed is not settled, because the statute doesn't define the word. There are two readings.
- One reading is that any failure to keep a listed item, such as the roof, in repair is material.
- The other reading is that it depends on how serious the problem is, how long it has gone on, and how it affects living there.
- Your facts for the second reading are a leak since March 20 that drips whenever it rains, two unanswered requests, and no repair.

### Did paying April rent give up your right?
- Section 83.56(5)(a) says that if a tenant "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord," the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance."
- You paid on April 1 knowing about the leak. Whether that matters is not settled, and there are two readings.
- One reading is that a leak still unrepaired is a "continuing noncompliance," so paying rent gave up nothing.
- The other reading is that paying with knowledge gave up the right to end the lease over this failure, and only a new failure would start it over.
- May rent is due May 1. Paying it while the leak continues raises the same question again.

### What if you leave without a valid termination?
- Your lease has no early termination fee or addendum.
- If you leave and the landlord treats it as a breach, section 83.595 lists the landlord's choices. They include ending the tenancy, re-renting the unit for your account, or holding you to the rent as it comes due.
- Which choice the landlord makes is the landlord's decision. I can't give you a single amount you would owe.

### Other things to do before you leave
- Section 83.49(5) asks for at least 7 days' written notice, by certified mail or hand delivery, before you move out. The notice must include an address where you can be reached. Your lease, section 6, also requires a written forwarding address.
- A code complaint is a separate step. Section 83.64 protects tenants from retaliation for a good-faith complaint to a code office or for a repair notice under section 83.56(1).
