answer:
**Short answer:** No, the office's demand doesn't look right on the facts you gave me. You're active duty and have PCS orders to San Diego, which is more than 35 miles away. You gave written notice with a copy of the orders. That lets you end the lease under the servicemember law, and the lease can't take that right away. You would owe rent only up to your termination date, May 31. You would not owe the $2,100 fee or rent through July.

The 30-day clock started when the office got your notice on April 6. The earliest termination date it allows is May 6. Your notice says May 31.

Has the office put its demand for the $2,100 and the July rent in writing, or only told you in person or by phone?

DETAILS

### Can you end the lease because of your orders?
- Florida law lets a servicemember end a rental agreement with written notice. The date in the notice must be "at least 30 days after the landlord's receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)).
- One of the listed situations must apply. One is being "required, pursuant to a permanent change of station orders, to move 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises" (83.682(1)(a)). You confirmed PCS orders to San Diego, more than 35 miles from the apartment.
- The notice must come with "a copy of the official military orders" or a letter signed by your commanding officer (83.682(2)). You confirmed you handed the office your written notice with a copy of your orders.
- The 30 days count from April 6, when you confirmed the office received the notice. The earliest effective date is May 6. Your notice names May 31 as the end date.
- Your lease says notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office" (lease clause 7). You handed it to the office, so you followed that clause too.

### What do you owe after you end the lease this way?
- You owe "the rent due under the rental agreement prorated to the effective date of the termination" (83.682(4)). Here that means rent up to May 31.
- The statute also says you are "not liable for any other rent or damages due to the early termination of the tenancy" (83.682(4)). That rules out rent for June and July.

### Does the Addendum A fee still apply?
- No. Addendum A is the early termination fee option, and you checked the box agreeing to $2,100. The fee is allowed under Fla. Stat. 83.595(4), which covers a tenant who chooses to end the lease early under that option.
- Your termination rests on a different law. The servicemember law says it "may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances" (83.682(5)). A lease or addendum can't make you pay the fee for using it.
- Lease clause 11 (30 days' notice plus the Addendum A amount) is also a contract term. It can't override 83.682.

### What could change this answer?
- Everything above depends on your notice and orders being what you described. If the copy you gave was not your official orders, or the notice was not delivered on April 6, tell me. That would change the analysis.
- The office could still dispute something other than the fee, such as rent already due or damage. Those are separate from the fee and the July rent, and I haven't seen anything about them.

Loaded wants_to_leave_early. Its instructions:

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the tenant wants to move out before the lease term ends. It rests on 83.595 (the landlord's choice of remedies), 83.49 (the deposit and the 7-day notice before leaving), 83.682 (servicemembers), 83.575 (notice at the end of a lease), and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If part of the reason for leaving is that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required, also load repair_not_made. A way out may run through that skill and 83.56(1).
- Check the other ways out the record points to: military orders (83.682, in this skill), and damage to the unit, such as a fire or a storm. 83.63 may be the relevant section for damage; there is no skill for it, so fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it.
- The statute leaves out some cases. The tool does not decide whether any of them applies; say what the words are and what you would need to know.
  - "This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)(b)). This is about the liquidated damages and early termination fee option below.
  - "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(5)). The lease cannot take away the servicemember option.
  - "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). College housing may be an example.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- Any term on notice before moving out early, next to the 7-day notice below.
- The date the lease term ends, next to the date the tenant plans to move out.
- The monthly rent, next to any early termination amount.
- Where and how the tenant's notice must be sent under the lease.
- Any early termination addendum, and whether roommates who stay on are liable for the whole rent.

### From the tenant

- What date do they plan to move out?
- Does the lease have a fixed end date (for example, a one-year lease), and what date does the term end?
- How much is the monthly rent? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- Why do they want to leave early, in their own words? Is part of the reason that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required?
- Does the lease, or another paper they signed with it, set an early termination fee or liquidated damages for leaving early? Where is that fee written (in a separate paper signed with the lease, only in the lease itself, in the lease and in a separate paper, or they do not know), and what amount does it set?
- Have they given the landlord anything in writing saying they are moving out? How did it reach the landlord (handed to the landlord or the office, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal request or message, a text message, or something else), and what date was it delivered?
- Are they a servicemember (including the National Guard or reserves) with military orders that affect where they live? If so, have they given the landlord a written notice of termination with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer, and what date did the landlord receive it?

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the tenant plans to move out. The 7 days' notice count back from it.
- For a servicemember, whether the termination notice with the orders was given, and the date the landlord received it. The 30 days count from that date.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- The lease and any early termination addendum.
- The written notice of leaving, with proof of certified mail or personal delivery.
- The forwarding address given to the landlord.
- For a servicemember, the orders or the commanding officer's letter sent with the notice.
- Move-out photos and the key return date.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do each of these and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below). A few conditions are outside the tool, such as the military orders themselves; say what the tenant must check.

Lease override to show: 83.49(5) begins "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), so read the lease's term on notice before moving out. The servicemember option cannot be changed by the lease (the exclusion above).

### End the lease as a servicemember with military orders, by written notice with the orders, effective at least 30 days after the landlord receives it (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The tenant is a servicemember: "Any servicemember may terminate his or her rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The tenant can tell you. If they say they are not one, this option is closed.
2. The orders meet one of the criteria the statute lists: "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). This is outside the tool: the tenant checks the military orders against the criteria in 83.682(1) (a permanent change of station of 35 miles or more, a discharge or release from active duty, orders into government quarters, temporary orders of more than 60 days to 35 miles or more away, and the others). See the third open question.

Steps, in order:

1. A written notice of termination to the landlord, with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer: "The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Ask whether the tenant has given it.
2. The termination takes effect at least 30 days after the landlord receives the notice: "at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The program's deadlines show the earliest date, counted from the date the landlord received the notice.

### Leave early and pay the early termination fee or liquidated damages the lease sets, in place of the landlord's other remedies (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4))

All three conditions must be met.

1. The tenant signed a separate addendum agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages when the lease was made: "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). It is met in either way:
   - The fee is written in a separate paper the tenant signed with the lease: "The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant can tell you. If they say the fee is written only in the lease itself, not in a separate paper, the landlord's other remedies in 83.595 apply.
   - Where the fee is written is not known yet. The tenant checks the papers signed with the lease for a separate one agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages.
2. The amount is no more than 2 months' rent: "if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant checks the amount the fee or liquidated damages come to, beside two months' rent.
3. For a fee, the lease asks for no more than 60 days' notice before the early termination: "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before an early termination with search_lease and say what it says. See the second open question.

The step: the notice the lease asks for, given to the landlord: "as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). If the tenant has already given a notice, ask whether it is the one the lease asks for before an early termination, in its time and way, and read that clause. Which remedy the landlord picks is open (the first open question).

### Give the landlord 7 days' written notice before leaving, by certified mail or in person, with an address, so the landlord stays held to the deposit's notice of a claim (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The last day to give that notice has not passed, or the notice already went out by it: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). It is met in either way:
   - The last day has not passed. Only the program's deadlines settle this. If they show it has passed, say so.
   - The notice already given went out by the last day, by certified mail or in person, with an address. Ask the date it reached the landlord, to put beside the last day the program's deadlines show.
2. The lease does not provide otherwise on notice before moving out: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before moving out early with search_lease and say what it says.

The step: the written notice, with the address where the tenant can be reached, delivered to the landlord by certified mail or in person: "which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).

- If the notice went by certified mail or by hand, ask the tenant to check that it gave the address where they can be reached.
- If it went by e-mail, it counts only as 83.505 allows. Ask whether the tenant and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and whether the notice gave the address. Read the lease's clause on notices to the landlord.
- If it went some other way, ask how it reached the landlord, beside the ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation. The program computes no date from a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.

- The tenant's 7 days' written notice before leaving. It counts back from the date the tenant plans to move out, not forward from the notice date. It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise (quoted above).
- The servicemember's earliest termination date. It counts from the date the landlord received the notice, and only when the servicemember notice was given: "written notice of termination to be effective on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)).

## What the statute does not settle

Each of these has no listed readings. For each, say what the tool does not work out, apply the text to what the tenant reports, and pick no answer for the law.

### Which remedy the landlord chooses

83.595 lists what the landlord may do when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, in four subsections: end the tenancy and the tenant's liability; relet for the tenant's account, where the landlord has "a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)); stand by and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee under a separate addendum. The choice is the landlord's. Lay the four beside what the record holds (the addendum, its amount, the monthly rent) so the tenant sees what each would mean. Never say which the landlord will choose, and never give one amount owed.

### The notice period for an early termination fee

83.595(4) refers to an early termination fee where "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The period comes from the lease, and the tool does not compute a date from a period the lease sets.

### Whether the servicemember criteria are met

83.682(1) applies only "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)), and 83.682(2) says the notice "must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Apply the criteria and the documents to what the tenant reports. A criterion the record does not show is not known yet.

### Damage to the unit

If the tenant is leaving because the unit was damaged or destroyed (for example, by fire or a storm), 83.63 may be the relevant section. There is no skill for it. Fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it, and say the tool does not compute anything for it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the planned move-out date, the forwarding address, what the tenant asks for, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that the program computes the 7-day date in 83.49(5), which requires "at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), counted back from the move-out date they gave. The letter is that notice only if it is sent that way and gives their new address.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating what the tenant will owe as one amount. 83.595 lists the landlord's choices.
- Applying 83.595(4)'s fee or liquidated damages without the separate addendum, which the tenant must accept "by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- Applying 83.595(2) without the landlord's "duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)).
- Missing a way out the record points to, such as the landlord's noncompliance (through the repair skill and 83.56(1)), military orders (83.682), or damage to the unit (83.63).
- Counting the 7 days from the notice date instead of back from the move-out date.
- Computing a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.result: 83.682 Termination of rental agreement by a servicemember. — (1) Any servicemember may terminate his or her rental agreement by providing the landlord with a written notice of termination to be effective on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice if any of the following criteria are met: (a) The servicemember is required, pursuant to a permanent change of station orders, to move 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises; (b) The servicemember is prematurely or involuntarily discharged or released from active duty or state active duty; (c) The servicemember is released from active duty or state active duty after having leased the rental premises while on active duty or state active duty status and the rental premises is 35 miles or more from the servicemember’s home of record before entering active duty or state active duty; (d) After entering into a rental agreement, the servicemember receives military orders requiring him or her to move into government quarters or the servicemember becomes eligible to live in and opts to move into government quarters. For purposes of this paragraph, the term “government quarters” means any military housing option that is available to a servicemember, including privatized military housing that is owned, operated, or managed by a private sector company; (e) The servicemember receives temporary duty orders, temporary change of station orders, or state active duty orders to an area 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises, provided such orders are for a period exceeding 60 days; or (f) The servicemember has leased the property, but before taking possession of the rental premises, receives a change of orders to an area that is 35 miles or more from the location of the rental premises. (2) The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer. (3) In the event a servicemember dies during active duty, an adult member of his or her immediate family may terminate the servicemember’s rental agreement by providing the landlord with a written notice of termination to be effective on the date stated in the notice that is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice. The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders showing the servicemember was on active duty or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer and a copy of the servicemember’s death certificate. (4) Upon termination of a rental agreement under this section, the tenant is liable for the rent due under the rental agreement prorated to the effective date of the termination payable at such time as would have otherwise been required by the terms of the rental agreement. The tenant is not liable for any other rent or damages due to the early termination of the tenancy as provided for in this section. Notwithstanding any provision of this section to the contrary, if a tenant terminates the rental agreement pursuant to this section 14 or more days prior to occupancy, no damages or penalties of any kind will be assessable. (5) The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances. History. — s. 6, ch. 2001-179; s. 1, ch. 2002-4; s. 1, ch. 2003-30; s. 5, ch. 2003-72; s. 1, ch. 2023-159.

answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not. The $1,500 charge and the lost deposit are in your lease, but Florida law only lets a landlord enforce a fixed early-leaving fee if you signed a separate paper agreeing to it. You told me you signed only the lease, so that fee option looks unavailable. Your landlord would still have other ways to charge you for leaving early. They are tied to the rent for the months left on the lease, which runs to July 31, 2026. I can't tell you which one your landlord will pick or give you a single dollar figure.

You should also give written notice before you go. The last day to do that is March 8, 2026, and that date has not passed. Will you give that notice by hand at the office or by certified mail?

DETAILS

### Is the $1,500 charge enforceable as written?
- Lease section 11 says that if you move out early you "shall pay Landlord a re-rental charge of $1,500.00, and the security deposit is forfeited to Landlord."
- Fla. Stat. 83.595(4) lets a landlord charge a fixed early-leaving fee or liquidated damages (an amount the parties agree on in advance) only in limited cases.
  - The amount can't be more than 2 months' rent. Your rent is $1,050, so $1,500 is under that limit.
  - The statute also says: "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee."
  - You show acceptance "by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement."
- Your lease puts the charge inside the lease, and you signed no addendum. On those facts, the 83.595(4) fee option doesn't appear to be open to your landlord.
- The statute does not say what happens to a charge written only in the lease. I would not treat section 11 as settled either way.
- Please check that nothing else was signed with the lease, such as an online form or a move-in packet page.

### What can your landlord do instead?
Under 83.595, once you surrender or abandon the apartment, the landlord chooses one of these:
1. **End the lease** and retake the apartment for themselves, which ends your further liability (83.595(1)).
2. **Re-rent the apartment on your account.** You would owe the difference between your rent and what the re-rental brings in. The landlord must use "good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (83.595(2)).
3. **Do nothing and hold you to the rent** as it comes due, at $1,050 a month (83.595(3)).
4. **Charge the fixed fee.** This needs the separate signed addendum, which you don't have.

What you owe depends on which of options 1 to 3 the landlord picks and on how quickly the apartment is re-rented.

### What about the deposit?
Section 11 says the deposit is forfeited. I have not looked at the deposit rules in 83.49 for this answer, so I can't say whether the landlord can keep it under that clause. Lease section 5 also says the deposit can't be used for your last month's rent.

### Do you have to give notice, and by when?
- The statute, 83.49(5), says a tenant must "give at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached."
- That section begins "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement." Your lease has no clause on notice before leaving early. Section 6 only says to give a forwarding address in writing at move-out.
- Counting back from your March 15 move-out date, the last day for the 7-day notice is March 8, 2026. That date has not passed.
- Lease section 7 says notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail." Email isn't an option under section 8.
- Missing the notice doesn't waive your right to the deposit. It does relieve the landlord of a notice duty that goes with the deposit (83.49(5)).

### Is there another way out of the lease?
Nothing you've told me points to one. You are leaving to be closer to work. I haven't heard of military orders, unit damage, or unfixed repairs. If any of those applies, tell me, because it could change the answer.

Load this skill when the tenant wants to move out before the lease term ends. It rests on 83.595 (the landlord's choice of remedies), 83.49 (the deposit and the 7-day notice before leaving), 83.682 (servicemembers), 83.575 (notice at the end of a lease), and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If part of the reason for leaving is that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required, also load repair_not_made. A way out may run through that skill and 83.56(1).
- Check the other ways out the record points to: military orders (83.682, in this skill), and damage to the unit, such as a fire or a storm. 83.63 may be the relevant section for damage; there is no skill for it, so fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it.
- The statute leaves out some cases. The tool does not decide whether any of them applies; say what the words are and what you would need to know.
  - "This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)(b)). This is about the liquidated damages and early termination fee option below.
  - "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(5)). The lease cannot take away the servicemember option.
  - "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). College housing may be an example.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- Any term on notice before moving out early, next to the 7-day notice below.
- The date the lease term ends, next to the date the tenant plans to move out.
- The monthly rent, next to any early termination amount.
- Where and how the tenant's notice must be sent under the lease.
- Any early termination addendum, and whether roommates who stay on are liable for the whole rent.

### From the tenant

- What date do they plan to move out?
- Does the lease have a fixed end date (for example, a one-year lease), and what date does the term end?
- How much is the monthly rent? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- Why do they want to leave early, in their own words? Is part of the reason that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required?
- Does the lease, or another paper they signed with it, set an early termination fee or liquidated damages for leaving early? Where is that fee written (in a separate paper signed with the lease, only in the lease itself, in the lease and in a separate paper, or they do not know), and what amount does it set?
- Have they given the landlord anything in writing saying they are moving out? How did it reach the landlord (handed to the landlord or the office, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal request or message, a text message, or something else), and what date was it delivered?
- Are they a servicemember (including the National Guard or reserves) with military orders that affect where they live? If so, have they given the landlord a written notice of termination with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer, and what date did the landlord receive it?

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the tenant plans to move out. The 7 days' notice count back from it.
- For a servicemember, whether the termination notice with the orders was given, and the date the landlord received it. The 30 days count from that date.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- The lease and any early termination addendum.
- The written notice of leaving, with proof of certified mail or personal delivery.
- The forwarding address given to the landlord.
- For a servicemember, the orders or the commanding officer's letter sent with the notice.
- Move-out photos and the key return date.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do each of these and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below). A few conditions are outside the tool, such as the military orders themselves; say what the tenant must check.

Lease override to show: 83.49(5) begins "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), so read the lease's term on notice before moving out. The servicemember option cannot be changed by the lease (the exclusion above).

### End the lease as a servicemember with military orders, by written notice with the orders, effective at least 30 days after the landlord receives it (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The tenant is a servicemember: "Any servicemember may terminate his or her rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The tenant can tell you. If they say they are not one, this option is closed.
2. The orders meet one of the criteria the statute lists: "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). This is outside the tool: the tenant checks the military orders against the criteria in 83.682(1) (a permanent change of station of 35 miles or more, a discharge or release from active duty, orders into government quarters, temporary orders of more than 60 days to 35 miles or more away, and the others). See the third open question.

Steps, in order:

1. A written notice of termination to the landlord, with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer: "The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Ask whether the tenant has given it.
2. The termination takes effect at least 30 days after the landlord receives the notice: "at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The program's deadlines show the earliest date, counted from the date the landlord received the notice.

All three conditions must be met.

1. The tenant signed a separate addendum agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages when the lease was made: "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). It is met in either way:
   - The fee is written in a separate paper the tenant signed with the lease: "The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. 2. The amount is no more than 2 months' rent: "if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant checks the amount the fee or liquidated damages come to, beside two months' rent.

For a fee, the lease asks for no more than 60 days' notice before the early termination: "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. If the tenant has already given a notice, ask whether it is the one the lease asks for before an early termination, in its time and way, and read that clause. Which remedy the landlord picks is open (the first open question).

### Give the landlord 7 days' written notice before leaving, by certified mail or in person, with an address, so the landlord stays held to the deposit's notice of a claim (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The last day to give that notice has not passed, or the notice already went out by it: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). It is met in either way:

2. The lease does not provide otherwise on notice before moving out: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before moving out early with search_lease and say what it says.

The step: the written notice, with the address where the tenant can be reached, delivered to the landlord by certified mail or in person: "which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).

- If it went some other way, ask how it reached the landlord, beside the ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation. The program computes no date from a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.

It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise (quoted above).
- The servicemember's earliest termination date. It counts from the date the landlord received the notice, and only when the servicemember notice was given: "written notice of termination to be effective on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)).

Each of these has no listed readings. For each, say what the tool does not work out, apply the text to what the tenant reports, and pick no answer for the law.

### Which remedy the landlord chooses

83.595 lists what the landlord may do when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, in four subsections: end the tenancy and the tenant's liability; relet for the tenant's account, where the landlord has "a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)); stand by and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee under a separate addendum. The choice is the landlord's. Lay the four beside what the record holds (the addendum, its amount, the monthly rent) so the tenant sees what each would mean. Never say which the landlord will choose, and never give one amount owed.

### The notice period for an early termination fee

83.595(4) refers to an early termination fee where "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The period comes from the lease, and the tool does not compute a date from a period the lease sets.

83.682(1) applies only "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)), and 83.682(2) says the notice "must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Apply the criteria and the documents to what the tenant reports. A criterion the record does not show is not known yet.

If the tenant is leaving because the unit was damaged or destroyed (for example, by fire or a storm), 83.63 may be the relevant section. There is no skill for it. Fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it, and say the tool does not compute anything for it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the planned move-out date, the forwarding address, what the tenant asks for, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted.

Stat. 83.49(5)), counted back from the move-out date they gave. The letter is that notice only if it is sent that way and gives their new address.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

- Stating what the tenant will owe as one amount. 83.595 lists the landlord's choices.

tool_calls.result: 83.595 Choice of remedies upon breach or early termination by tenant. — If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord, or the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit, the landlord may: (1) Treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for his or her own account, thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant; (2) Retake possession of the dwelling unit for the account of the tenant, holding the tenant liable for the difference between the rent stipulated to be paid under the rental agreement and what the landlord is able to recover from a reletting. If the landlord retakes possession, the landlord has a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises, and any rent received by the landlord as a result of the reletting must be deducted from the balance of rent due from the tenant. For purposes of this subsection, the term “good faith in attempting to relet the premises” means that the landlord uses at least the same efforts to relet the premises as were used in the initial rental or at least the same efforts as the landlord uses in attempting to rent other similar rental units but does not require the landlord to give a preference in renting the premises over other vacant dwelling units that the landlord owns or has the responsibility to rent; (3) Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due; or (4) Charge liquidated damages, as provided in the rental agreement, or an early termination fee to the tenant if the landlord and tenant have agreed to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent, and if, in the case of an early termination fee, the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination. This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee. The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement containing a provision in substantially the following form: ☐ I agree, as provided in the rental agreement, to pay $ (an amount that does not exceed 2 months’ rent) as liquidated damages or an early termination fee if I elect to terminate the rental agreement, and the landlord waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession. ☐ I do not agree to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, and I acknowledge that the landlord may seek damages as provided by law. (a) In addition to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, the landlord is entitled to the rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession of the dwelling unit and charges for damages to the dwelling unit. (b) This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 . History. — s. 2, ch. 87-369; s. 4, ch. 88-379; s. 448, ch. 95-147; s. 2, ch. 2008-131.

answer:
Yes, you likely have two options under Florida's casualty law. The fire began next door, and you didn't cause it. You can end the lease and move out right away. Or you can give up only the kitchen and living room and pay less rent. Ending the lease depends on whether your home is "substantially impaired." That point isn't settled, so I can't promise it. Your lease doesn't mention fire or damage, so it doesn't change either option. The statute doesn't set a formula for the rent cut. Have you told your landlord about the damage in writing yet? If so, how did you send it?

DETAILS

### Does the casualty law apply to your fire?
Section 83.63 applies if the home is damaged "other than by the wrongful or negligent acts of the tenant so that the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired." The fire department's report says the fire began in the apartment next door. Nothing you've told me suggests you caused it. You confirmed that smoke and water left the kitchen and living room unusable.

### Can you end the lease?
Section 83.63(1) says the tenant "may terminate the rental agreement and immediately vacate the premises."
- **Your side:** You can't use the kitchen or the living room, so you can't cook or sit in your own home. That supports a claim of substantial impairment.
- **Landlord's side:** The landlord could say the bedroom and bathroom still work, so the impairment isn't substantial.
- The statute doesn't say how much damage counts. I can't tell you which reading a court would pick.
- If you end the lease, the landlord must handle your deposit under s. 83.49(3). That is the section 83.63(1) points to.

### Can you pay less and stay?
Section 83.63(1) also says the tenant "may vacate the part of the premises rendered unusable by the casualty, in which case the tenant's liability for rent shall be reduced by the fair rental value of that part of the premises damaged or destroyed."
- You could stop using the kitchen and living room and keep the bedroom and bathroom. Your rent of $1,050.00 a month (lease §4) would drop by what those two rooms are fairly worth to rent.
- The statute doesn't say how to work out that value, and the tool doesn't either. The landlord might dispute the number.
- You paid May rent on May 1, before the fire. I don't yet know about rent due since then.

### Do you have to follow the lease's notice rules?
Section 83.63 doesn't say how to tell the landlord. Lease §7 says written notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail." Using that method is the safest way to prove what you told the landlord.

### What if you move out?
Section 83.63(2) says you must be given a chance to collect your belongings when it is safe. Or you must be told the date you can collect them, which must be within a reasonable time.

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the tenant wants to move out before the lease term ends. It rests on 83.595 (the landlord's choice of remedies), 83.49 (the deposit and the 7-day notice before leaving), 83.682 (servicemembers), 83.575 (notice at the end of a lease), and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If part of the reason for leaving is that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required, also load repair_not_made. A way out may run through that skill and 83.56(1).
- Check the other ways out the record points to: military orders (83.682, in this skill), and damage to the unit, such as a fire or a storm. 83.63 may be the relevant section for damage; there is no skill for it, so fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it.
- The statute leaves out some cases. The tool does not decide whether any of them applies; say what the words are and what you would need to know.
  - "This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)(b)). This is about the liquidated damages and early termination fee option below.
  - "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(5)). The lease cannot take away the servicemember option.
  - "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). College housing may be an example.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- Any term on notice before moving out early, next to the 7-day notice below.
- The date the lease term ends, next to the date the tenant plans to move out.
- The monthly rent, next to any early termination amount.
- Where and how the tenant's notice must be sent under the lease.
- Any early termination addendum, and whether roommates who stay on are liable for the whole rent.

### From the tenant

- What date do they plan to move out?
- Does the lease have a fixed end date (for example, a one-year lease), and what date does the term end?
- How much is the monthly rent? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- Why do they want to leave early, in their own words? Is part of the reason that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required?
- Does the lease, or another paper they signed with it, set an early termination fee or liquidated damages for leaving early? - Are they a servicemember (including the National Guard or reserves) with military orders that affect where they live? If so, have they given the landlord a written notice of termination with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer, and what date did the landlord receive it?

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the tenant plans to move out. The 7 days' notice count back from it.

- The written notice of leaving, with proof of certified mail or personal delivery.

Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below). Both conditions must be met.

1. The tenant is a servicemember: "Any servicemember may terminate his or her rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The tenant can tell you. If they say they are not one, this option is closed.
2. The orders meet one of the criteria the statute lists: "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). This is outside the tool: the tenant checks the military orders against the criteria in 83.682(1) (a permanent change of station of 35 miles or more, a discharge or release from active duty, orders into government quarters, temporary orders of more than 60 days to 35 miles or more away, and the others). See the third open question.

A written notice of termination to the landlord, with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer: "The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer." Both conditions must be met.

1. The last day to give that notice has not passed, or the notice already went out by it: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). It is met in either way:

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Stat. 83.595(4)). The period comes from the lease, and the tool does not compute a date from a period the lease sets.

answer:
**Short answer:** Probably not the full $3,000, but I can't tell you the exact amount. Florida law lets a landlord charge an early termination fee only if it is no more than two months' rent. Your rent is $1,050, so the cap is $2,100, and $3,000 is over it. That means your landlord likely can't rely on the fee remedy in the statute. Your landlord still has other ways to seek money, and it's unsettled how a court would treat your signed addendum. Nothing is owed yet, because you haven't left.

Your lease also has its own early-exit clause. It asks for 30 days' written notice, delivered by hand or certified mail to the office. For an April 30 move-out, the last day for that notice is March 31, 2026. That date hasn't passed.

What is your plan for delivering the notice: by hand to Suite A, or by certified mail?

DETAILS

### Is the $3,000 fee allowed under the statute?
- Your addendum is a separate signed paper with the fee box checked, as the statute requires (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- The statute allows the fee remedy only "if the amount does not exceed 2 months' rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- Two months of your rent is $2,100, and the addendum sets $3,000.
- The statute's form of addendum says the amount must be "an amount that does not exceed 2 months' rent." Yours does not meet that.
- So the fee remedy in subsection (4) is likely not available to your landlord at $3,000.

### What can your landlord do instead?
When a tenant leaves early, the statute lets the landlord pick one of four remedies (Fla. Stat. 83.595):
1. Treat the lease as ended and end your liability.
2. Retake the unit for your account and relet it. Your landlord must act in good faith to relet, and any rent received reduces what you owe.
3. Stand by and hold you liable for the rent as it comes due.
4. Charge the agreed fee, if it meets the limits above.

The choice is your landlord's, and I can't say which one it will pick. Under options 2 or 3, you could owe rent beyond April, up to the lease end on July 31, 2026. That could be more or less than $3,000, depending on reletting.

### Does the lease or the addendum change this?
- Clause 11 lets you end the lease early by giving "30 days' written notice, delivered as clause 7 says, and paying the amount Tenant agreed to in Addendum A."
- Landlord's reading: you agreed to $3,000 as the price of leaving, so you owe it.
- Your reading: the statute caps the fee at two months' rent, and the fee remedy is "available only if" the cap is met. So $3,000 can't be enforced as written.
- The statute doesn't say whether a court would cut the fee to $2,100, throw out the addendum, or enforce the amount. I can't pick one.
- If the addendum did hold, it says your landlord "waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession." Under the statute, you would still owe rent and charges through the end of the month your landlord retakes possession (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)(a)).

### What notice should you give, and by when?
- Lease clause 7 says notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or "sent there by certified mail." E-mail and portal messages are not listed.
- For the lease's 30-day notice, the program counts back from your April 30 move-out to March 31, 2026, which has not passed.
- Separately, the deposit statute asks for at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery before you leave, with an address where you can be reached (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). That counts back to April 23, 2026, which has not passed.
- One letter delivered by hand or certified mail, with your new address and April 30 as the move-out date, can serve both purposes. Sending it by the earlier date covers both.
- Keep proof of delivery.

Load this skill when the tenant wants to move out before the lease term ends. It rests on 83.595 (the landlord's choice of remedies), 83.49 (the deposit and the 7-day notice before leaving), 83.682 (servicemembers), 83.575 (notice at the end of a lease), and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If part of the reason for leaving is that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required, also load repair_not_made. A way out may run through that skill and 83.56(1).
- Check the other ways out the record points to: military orders (83.682, in this skill), and damage to the unit, such as a fire or a storm. 83.63 may be the relevant section for damage; there is no skill for it, so fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it.
- The statute leaves out some cases. The tool does not decide whether any of them applies; say what the words are and what you would need to know.
  - "This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)(b)). This is about the liquidated damages and early termination fee option below.
  - "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(5)). The lease cannot take away the servicemember option.
  - "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). College housing may be an example.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- Any term on notice before moving out early, next to the 7-day notice below.
- The date the lease term ends, next to the date the tenant plans to move out.
- The monthly rent, next to any early termination amount.
- Where and how the tenant's notice must be sent under the lease.
- Any early termination addendum, and whether roommates who stay on are liable for the whole rent.

### From the tenant

- What date do they plan to move out?
- Does the lease have a fixed end date (for example, a one-year lease), and what date does the term end?
- How much is the monthly rent? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- Why do they want to leave early, in their own words? Is part of the reason that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required?
- Does the lease, or another paper they signed with it, set an early termination fee or liquidated damages for leaving early? Where is that fee written (in a separate paper signed with the lease, only in the lease itself, in the lease and in a separate paper, or they do not know), and what amount does it set?
- Have they given the landlord anything in writing saying they are moving out? How did it reach the landlord (handed to the landlord or the office, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal request or message, a text message, or something else), and what date was it delivered?
- Are they a servicemember (including the National Guard or reserves) with military orders that affect where they live? If so, have they given the landlord a written notice of termination with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer, and what date did the landlord receive it?

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the tenant plans to move out. The 7 days' notice count back from it.
- For a servicemember, whether the termination notice with the orders was given, and the date the landlord received it. The 30 days count from that date.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- The lease and any early termination addendum.
- The written notice of leaving, with proof of certified mail or personal delivery.
- The forwarding address given to the landlord.
- For a servicemember, the orders or the commanding officer's letter sent with the notice.
- Move-out photos and the key return date.

## What the tenant can do

Tell the tenant first whether they can do each of these and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below). A few conditions are outside the tool, such as the military orders themselves; say what the tenant must check.

Lease override to show: 83.49(5) begins "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), so read the lease's term on notice before moving out. The servicemember option cannot be changed by the lease (the exclusion above).

### End the lease as a servicemember with military orders, by written notice with the orders, effective at least 30 days after the landlord receives it (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The tenant is a servicemember: "Any servicemember may terminate his or her rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The tenant can tell you. If they say they are not one, this option is closed.
2. The orders meet one of the criteria the statute lists: "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). This is outside the tool: the tenant checks the military orders against the criteria in 83.682(1) (a permanent change of station of 35 miles or more, a discharge or release from active duty, orders into government quarters, temporary orders of more than 60 days to 35 miles or more away, and the others). See the third open question.

Steps, in order:

1. A written notice of termination to the landlord, with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer: "The notice to the landlord must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Ask whether the tenant has given it.
2. The termination takes effect at least 30 days after the landlord receives the notice: "at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)). The program's deadlines show the earliest date, counted from the date the landlord received the notice.

### Leave early and pay the early termination fee or liquidated damages the lease sets, in place of the landlord's other remedies (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4))

All three conditions must be met.

1. The tenant signed a separate addendum agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages when the lease was made: "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). It is met in either way:
   - The fee is written in a separate paper the tenant signed with the lease: "The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant can tell you. If they say the fee is written only in the lease itself, not in a separate paper, the landlord's other remedies in 83.595 apply.
   - Where the fee is written is not known yet. The tenant checks the papers signed with the lease for a separate one agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages.
2. The amount is no more than 2 months' rent: "if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant checks the amount the fee or liquidated damages come to, beside two months' rent.
3. For a fee, the lease asks for no more than 60 days' notice before the early termination: "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before an early termination with search_lease and say what it says. See the second open question.

The step: the notice the lease asks for, given to the landlord: "as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). If the tenant has already given a notice, ask whether it is the one the lease asks for before an early termination, in its time and way, and read that clause. Which remedy the landlord picks is open (the first open question).

### Give the landlord 7 days' written notice before leaving, by certified mail or in person, with an address, so the landlord stays held to the deposit's notice of a claim (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The last day to give that notice has not passed, or the notice already went out by it: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). It is met in either way:
   - The last day has not passed. Only the program's deadlines settle this. If they show it has passed, say so.
   - The notice already given went out by the last day, by certified mail or in person, with an address. Ask the date it reached the landlord, to put beside the last day the program's deadlines show.
2. The lease does not provide otherwise on notice before moving out: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before moving out early with search_lease and say what it says.

The step: the written notice, with the address where the tenant can be reached, delivered to the landlord by certified mail or in person: "which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).

- If the notice went by certified mail or by hand, ask the tenant to check that it gave the address where they can be reached.
- If it went by e-mail, it counts only as 83.505 allows. Ask whether the tenant and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and whether the notice gave the address. Read the lease's clause on notices to the landlord.
- If it went some other way, ask how it reached the landlord, beside the ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation. The program computes no date from a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.

- The tenant's 7 days' written notice before leaving. It counts back from the date the tenant plans to move out, not forward from the notice date. It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise (quoted above).
- The servicemember's earliest termination date. It counts from the date the landlord received the notice, and only when the servicemember notice was given: "written notice of termination to be effective on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)).

## What the statute does not settle

Each of these has no listed readings. For each, say what the tool does not work out, apply the text to what the tenant reports, and pick no answer for the law.

### Which remedy the landlord chooses

83.595 lists what the landlord may do when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, in four subsections: end the tenancy and the tenant's liability; relet for the tenant's account, where the landlord has "a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)); stand by and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee under a separate addendum. The choice is the landlord's. Lay the four beside what the record holds (the addendum, its amount, the monthly rent) so the tenant sees what each would mean. Never say which the landlord will choose, and never give one amount owed.

### The notice period for an early termination fee

83.595(4) refers to an early termination fee where "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The period comes from the lease, and the tool does not compute a date from a period the lease sets.

### Whether the servicemember criteria are met

83.682(1) applies only "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)), and 83.682(2) says the notice "must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Apply the criteria and the documents to what the tenant reports. A criterion the record does not show is not known yet.

### Damage to the unit

If the tenant is leaving because the unit was damaged or destroyed (for example, by fire or a storm), 83.63 may be the relevant section. There is no skill for it. Fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it, and say the tool does not compute anything for it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the planned move-out date, the forwarding address, what the tenant asks for, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that the program computes the 7-day date in 83.49(5), which requires "at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), counted back from the move-out date they gave. The letter is that notice only if it is sent that way and gives their new address.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating what the tenant will owe as one amount. 83.595 lists the landlord's choices.
- Applying 83.595(4)'s fee or liquidated damages without the separate addendum, which the tenant must accept "by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- Applying 83.595(2) without the landlord's "duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)).
- Missing a way out the record points to, such as the landlord's noncompliance (through the repair skill and 83.56(1)), military orders (83.682), or damage to the unit (83.63).
- Counting the 7 days from the notice date instead of back from the move-out date.
- Computing a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.result: 83.595 Choice of remedies upon breach or early termination by tenant. — If the tenant breaches the rental agreement for the dwelling unit and the landlord has obtained a writ of possession, or the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord, or the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit, the landlord may: (1) Treat the rental agreement as terminated and retake possession for his or her own account, thereby terminating any further liability of the tenant; (2) Retake possession of the dwelling unit for the account of the tenant, holding the tenant liable for the difference between the rent stipulated to be paid under the rental agreement and what the landlord is able to recover from a reletting. If the landlord retakes possession, the landlord has a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises, and any rent received by the landlord as a result of the reletting must be deducted from the balance of rent due from the tenant. For purposes of this subsection, the term “good faith in attempting to relet the premises” means that the landlord uses at least the same efforts to relet the premises as were used in the initial rental or at least the same efforts as the landlord uses in attempting to rent other similar rental units but does not require the landlord to give a preference in renting the premises over other vacant dwelling units that the landlord owns or has the responsibility to rent; (3) Stand by and do nothing, holding the lessee liable for the rent as it comes due; or (4) Charge liquidated damages, as provided in the rental agreement, or an early termination fee to the tenant if the landlord and tenant have agreed to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent, and if, in the case of an early termination fee, the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination. This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee. The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement containing a provision in substantially the following form: ☐ I agree, as provided in the rental agreement, to pay $ (an amount that does not exceed 2 months’ rent) as liquidated damages or an early termination fee if I elect to terminate the rental agreement, and the landlord waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession. ☐ I do not agree to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, and I acknowledge that the landlord may seek damages as provided by law. (a) In addition to liquidated damages or an early termination fee, the landlord is entitled to the rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession of the dwelling unit and charges for damages to the dwelling unit. (b) This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 . History. — s. 2, ch. 87-369; s. 4, ch. 88-379; s. 448, ch. 95-147; s. 2, ch. 2008-131.

answer:
**Short answer:** Based on the addendum you signed, you would owe a flat $2,100.00 early termination fee, which is two months' rent. You would also owe rent through the end of the month the landlord retakes the apartment, plus any charge for damage. In return, the landlord gives up the right to seek further rent beyond that month. First, you have to give the landlord 30 days' written notice, delivered the way the lease requires. Counting back from May 31, the tool shows May 1 as that date. I can't tell you the landlord will pick this option, because the law lets the landlord choose among several remedies. Your lease and addendum point to the fee.

How will you deliver the notice: by hand to the office, or by certified mail?

DETAILS

### Does the early termination fee apply to you?
- The law lets a landlord charge an early termination fee only if you both agreed to it when the lease was made. You must have agreed by signing a separate addendum (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- Your Addendum A is a separate page. You signed and dated it July 10, 2025, the same day as the lease. The box you marked says you agree "to pay $2,100.00 as liquidated damages or an early termination fee." The box saying you do not agree is unmarked.
- The fee can't exceed 2 months' rent (83.595(4)). Your rent is $1,050.00 (lease clause 4), so two months is $2,100.00. The fee is exactly at the limit, not over it.
- For a fee, the lease can't require more than 60 days' notice (83.595(4)). Clause 11 requires 30 days, so it is within the limit.
- The exception for failing to give end-of-lease notice (83.595(4)(b), referring to 83.575) doesn't fit your situation. You are leaving before the lease ends, not failing to give notice at its end.

### What else could you owe on top of the fee?
- Besides the fee, the landlord is entitled to "rent and other charges accrued through the end of the month in which the landlord retakes possession" and to charges for damage to the unit (83.595(4)(a)).
- If the landlord retakes the apartment after May 31, you could owe rent into that later month. When the landlord retakes it is unknown.
- The addendum says the landlord "waives the right to seek additional rent beyond the month in which the landlord retakes possession."

### Could the landlord choose a different remedy?
- The law lists four options for a landlord when a tenant leaves early (83.595):
  - End the lease and your liability.
  - Re-rent the unit for your account and charge you any shortfall. The landlord must make a good-faith effort to re-rent.
  - Wait and charge you rent as it comes due.
  - Charge the agreed fee.
- Your signed addendum points to the fee. The addendum is worded as your choice ("if I elect to terminate").
- The statute doesn't say whether the landlord could pick another option anyway. Reading it one way, the landlord is held to what was agreed. Reading it the other way, the landlord chooses among the four. This tool can't settle that.

### What must you do first?
- **Written notice under the lease.** Clause 11 requires 30 days' written notice, "delivered as clause 7 says." Clause 7 says to deliver it "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail." Email or the resident portal does not fit that clause. Clause 8 also says you have not agreed to email notices.
- **Deadline.** Counting back 30 days from May 31, the tool shows May 1, 2026. That date has not passed. The tool counts calendar days and hasn't checked the counting method against the law. Deliver well before May 1 to be safe.
- **Statutory 7-day notice.** The law also requires at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery. It must include the address where you can be reached (83.49(5)). The tool shows May 24 as the last day. Your 30-day notice can cover both if it includes your forwarding address.
- **Why the 7-day notice matters.** If you skip it, the landlord is relieved of the 30-day deadline to notify you of a claim on your deposit. You keep your right to the deposit (83.49(5)).
- **Forwarding address.** Clause 6 also requires you to give your forwarding address in writing, return all keys to the office, and leave the apartment clean and empty.

### What should you keep?
- Keep a copy of the notice and your proof of delivery, either the certified mail receipt or a signed receipt from the office.
- Keep your copies of the lease and Addendum A.
- Keep move-out photos and a record of the date you returned the keys.
