2. The lease does not provide otherwise on notice before moving out: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before moving out early with search_lease and say what it says.

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation. The program computes no date from a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.

- The servicemember's earliest termination date. 83.595 lists what the landlord may do when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, in four subsections: end the tenancy and the tenant's liability; relet for the tenant's account, where the landlord has "a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)); stand by and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee under a separate addendum. The choice is the landlord's. Lay the four beside what the record holds (the addendum, its amount, the monthly rent) so the tenant sees what each would mean. Never say which the landlord will choose, and never give one amount owed.

### The notice period for an early termination fee

83.595(4) refers to an early termination fee where "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The period comes from the lease, and the tool does not compute a date from a period the lease sets.

### Whether the servicemember criteria are met

83.682(1) applies only "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)), and 83.682(2) says the notice "must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Apply the criteria and the documents to what the tenant reports. A criterion the record does not show is not known yet.

### Damage to the unit

If the tenant is leaving because the unit was damaged or destroyed (for example, by fire or a storm), 83.63 may be the relevant section. There is no skill for it. Fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it, and say the tool does not compute anything for it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the planned move-out date, the forwarding address, what the tenant asks for, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that the program computes the 7-day date in 83.49(5), which requires "at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), counted back from the move-out date they gave. The letter is that notice only if it is sent that way and gives their new address.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating what the tenant will owe as one amount. 83.595 lists the landlord's choices.
- Applying 83.595(4)'s fee or liquidated damages without the separate addendum, which the tenant must accept "by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- Applying 83.595(2) without the landlord's "duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)).
- Missing a way out the record points to, such as the landlord's noncompliance (through the repair skill and 83.56(1)), military orders (83.682), or damage to the unit (83.63).
- Counting the 7 days from the notice date instead of back from the move-out date.
- Computing a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.
- Computing any date yourself.

answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, it looks like you can end your lease. Your landlord never gave you the flood disclosure, and your losses meet the law's "substantial loss" test. The test is met because replacing your things would cost more than half of what they were worth. To use this, you must give written notice and hand back the apartment by July 20, 2026. That date has not passed. The lease ends when you hand back possession, not when you send the notice. Can you move out and return the keys by July 20?

DETAILS

### Did your landlord have to give you a flood disclosure?
- Under Fla. Stat. 83.512(1), a landlord "must complete and provide a flood disclosure to a prospective tenant of residential real property at or before the execution of a rental agreement for a term of 1 year or longer." It must be a separate document.
- Your lease runs from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026 (lease §3). That is a one-year term, so the rule appears to apply. A landlord could argue that a term ending December 31 is not a full year, but that argument looks weak.
- You confirmed you were never given a flood disclosure, and the lease has none.

### Is your loss big enough?
- Section 83.512(2) defines "substantial loss or damage" as a case where "the total cost of repairs to or replacement of the personal property is 50 percent or more of the personal property's market value on the date the flooding occurred."
- You confirmed that replacement would cost about $4,000 and the items were worth about $3,000 on June 20. The cost is above the value, so the 50% test is met.
- This covers your personal property, such as furniture and electronics. It does not cover the apartment itself.

### What must you do, and by when?
- Section 83.512(2) lets you end the lease "by giving a written notice of termination and surrendering possession of the premises to the landlord no later than 30 days after the date of the damage or loss."
- Counting from June 20, that deadline is July 20, 2026. Today is July 2, so it has not passed.
- Termination "is effective upon the tenant surrendering possession." Giving notice alone does not end the lease. You also have to move out and hand the apartment back.
- Lease §7 says written notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail." Use one of those two ways. Certified mail takes time, so hand delivery may be safer given the July 20 deadline. Lease §8 says the parties did not agree to e-mail notices, so do not rely on e-mail.

### What happens to rent and money you paid?
- Under 83.512(3), your landlord must refund "all rent or other amounts paid in advance" for any period after the termination takes effect.
- Under 83.512(4), you still owe any unpaid rent or other sums you owed before the termination date.
- Your security deposit is a separate matter. It is governed by 83.49 and the lease (§5, §6). Give your landlord a forwarding address in writing, as lease §6 requires.

### Is there another way out?
- Section 83.63 covers damage to the home from something other than the tenant's own fault. If the damage "substantially impaired" your enjoyment of the home, you may end the lease and move out right away. You may instead leave only the unusable part, and your rent drops by the fair rental value of that part.
- Whether this applies depends on the state of the apartment itself. That includes whether the flood left it unlivable or partly unusable. I don't have that fact yet.
- If it applies, 83.63(2) also gives you the right to collect your belongings when it is safe, or to be told the date you can collect them.
- This route has no 30-day cutoff in its text. The flood disclosure route is the one with a clear deadline, so treat July 20 as the date to meet.

For a fee, the lease asks for no more than 60 days' notice before the early termination: "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before an early termination with search_lease and say what it says. See the second open question.

The step: the notice the lease asks for, given to the landlord: "as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). If the tenant has already given a notice, ask whether it is the one the lease asks for before an early termination, in its time and way, and read that clause. Which remedy the landlord picks is open (the first open question).

### Give the landlord 7 days' written notice before leaving, by certified mail or in person, with an address, so the landlord stays held to the deposit's notice of a claim (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The last day to give that notice has not passed, or the notice already went out by it: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). It is met in either way:
   - The last day has not passed. Only the program's deadlines settle this. If they show it has passed, say so.
   - The notice already given went out by the last day, by certified mail or in person, with an address. Ask the date it reached the landlord, to put beside the last day the program's deadlines show.
2. The lease does not provide otherwise on notice before moving out: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before moving out early with search_lease and say what it says.

The step: the written notice, with the address where the tenant can be reached, delivered to the landlord by certified mail or in person: "which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).

- If the notice went by certified mail or by hand, ask the tenant to check that it gave the address where they can be reached.
- If it went by e-mail, it counts only as 83.505 allows. Ask whether the tenant and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and whether the notice gave the address. Read the lease's clause on notices to the landlord.
- If it went some other way, ask how it reached the landlord, beside the ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation. The program computes no date from a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.

- The tenant's 7 days' written notice before leaving. It counts back from the date the tenant plans to move out, not forward from the notice date. It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise (quoted above).
- The servicemember's earliest termination date. It counts from the date the landlord received the notice, and only when the servicemember notice was given: "written notice of termination to be effective on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)).

## What the statute does not settle

Each of these has no listed readings. For each, say what the tool does not work out, apply the text to what the tenant reports, and pick no answer for the law.

### Which remedy the landlord chooses

83.595 lists what the landlord may do when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, in four subsections: end the tenancy and the tenant's liability; relet for the tenant's account, where the landlord has "a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)); stand by and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee under a separate addendum. The choice is the landlord's. Lay the four beside what the record holds (the addendum, its amount, the monthly rent) so the tenant sees what each would mean. Never say which the landlord will choose, and never give one amount owed.

### The notice period for an early termination fee

83.595(4) refers to an early termination fee where "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The period comes from the lease, and the tool does not compute a date from a period the lease sets.

### Whether the servicemember criteria are met

83.682(1) applies only "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)), and 83.682(2) says the notice "must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Apply the criteria and the documents to what the tenant reports. A criterion the record does not show is not known yet.

### Damage to the unit

If the tenant is leaving because the unit was damaged or destroyed (for example, by fire or a storm), 83.63 may be the relevant section. There is no skill for it. Fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it, and say the tool does not compute anything for it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the planned move-out date, the forwarding address, what the tenant asks for, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that the program computes the 7-day date in 83.49(5), which requires "at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), counted back from the move-out date they gave. The letter is that notice only if it is sent that way and gives their new address.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating what the tenant will owe as one amount. 83.595 lists the landlord's choices.
- Applying 83.595(4)'s fee or liquidated damages without the separate addendum, which the tenant must accept "by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- Applying 83.595(2) without the landlord's "duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)).
- Missing a way out the record points to, such as the landlord's noncompliance (through the repair skill and 83.56(1)), military orders (83.682), or damage to the unit (83.63).
- Counting the 7 days from the notice date instead of back from the move-out date.
- Computing a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.
- Computing any date yourself.

answer:
**Short answer:** You likely can get out of your lease, or pay less rent while you stay. Florida law gives a tenant both choices when a fire or similar event, not caused by the tenant, badly damages the home. Your facts fit this. The fire department says it started next door, and your kitchen and living room can't be used. You can end the lease and move out right away. Or you can give up only the unusable rooms and keep paying rent reduced by what those rooms are fairly worth. The law doesn't set a dollar amount for that reduction. Your landlord could argue that the damage isn't serious enough to count, because you can still use two rooms. Which do you want: to move out completely, or to stay in the bedroom and bathroom at lower rent?

DETAILS

### Does the fire law apply to you?
- Section 83.63 applies if the home is damaged "other than by the wrongful or negligent acts of the tenant so that the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired."
- You told me the fire department's report says the fire began in the apartment next door. Nothing you've told me suggests you caused it. If your landlord says you did, that would change the answer.
- "Substantially impaired" isn't defined in the statute. Your side: you have no kitchen or living room, and the smoke and water damage makes the home hard to live in. Landlord's side: the bedroom and bathroom are still usable. The statute doesn't say which reading wins, so this point is open.

### Can you end the lease?
- Section 83.63(1) says the tenant "may terminate the rental agreement and immediately vacate the premises."
- Your lease doesn't mention fire or damage. The only clause that comes near is Section 3, which sets the end date of July 31, 2026. It doesn't limit your rights under 83.63.
- If you end the lease, the landlord must handle your security deposit under 83.49(3), as 83.63(1) says.
- Section 83.63(2) says you must get a chance to collect your belongings when it is safe. Otherwise you must get notice of a date, within a reasonable time, by which you can collect them.

### Can you pay less?
- Section 83.63(1) also says the tenant "may vacate the part of the premises rendered unusable by the casualty, in which case the tenant’s liability for rent shall be reduced by the fair rental value of that part of the premises damaged or destroyed."
- That fits your situation: you give up the kitchen and living room, keep the bedroom and bathroom, and owe less rent.
- The statute doesn't give a formula for "fair rental value." Your rent is $1,050.00 a month (Lease Section 4), but I can't tell you what share belongs to the damaged rooms. You and your landlord may disagree on that.
- You paid May rent on May 1, before the fire. Whether you can get part of it back or credited is not something the statute spells out.

### How should you tell your landlord?
- Section 83.63 doesn't say how to give notice.
- Lease Section 7 says written notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail." Using that method is the safest way to show your landlord got it.
- If you decide to leave, the written notice should also say where you can be reached. That keeps the deposit rules clear. Lease Section 6 also asks for a forwarding address in writing.

The tool doesn't calculate dates or dollar amounts under 83.63, so I haven't given any.

## When to load this skill

Load this skill when the tenant wants to move out before the lease term ends. It rests on 83.595 (the landlord's choice of remedies), 83.49 (the deposit and the 7-day notice before leaving), 83.682 (servicemembers), 83.575 (notice at the end of a lease), and 83.505 (notices by e-mail).

- If part of the reason for leaving is that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required, also load repair_not_made. A way out may run through that skill and 83.56(1).
- Check the other ways out the record points to: military orders (83.682, in this skill), and damage to the unit, such as a fire or a storm. 83.63 may be the relevant section for damage; there is no skill for it, so fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it.
- The statute leaves out some cases. The tool does not decide whether any of them applies; say what the words are and what you would need to know.
  - "This subsection does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)(b)). This is about the liquidated damages and early termination fee option below.
  - "The provisions of this section may not be waived or modified by the agreement of the parties under any circumstances." (Fla. Stat. 83.682(5)). The lease cannot take away the servicemember option.
  - "Residency or detention in a facility, whether public or private, when residence or detention is incidental to the provision of medical, geriatric, educational, counseling, religious, or similar services." (Fla. Stat. 83.42(1)). College housing may be an example.

## What to find out

Read the lease first, then ask the tenant. Ask what they saw, did, or hold, one or two things at a time and only what your answer turns on. Never ask whether something meets a term of the statute or the lease; ask what happened, then apply the term yourself.

### In the lease (search_lease; try a second wording if the first finds nothing)

- Any term on notice before moving out early, next to the 7-day notice below.
- The date the lease term ends, next to the date the tenant plans to move out.
- The monthly rent, next to any early termination amount.
- Where and how the tenant's notice must be sent under the lease.
- Any early termination addendum, and whether roommates who stay on are liable for the whole rent.

### From the tenant

- What date do they plan to move out?
- Does the lease have a fixed end date (for example, a one-year lease), and what date does the term end?
- How much is the monthly rent? (Only if the lease does not show it.)
- Why do they want to leave early, in their own words? Is part of the reason that the landlord has not made repairs or kept the unit as required?
- Does the lease, or another paper they signed with it, set an early termination fee or liquidated damages for leaving early? Where is that fee written (in a separate paper signed with the lease, only in the lease itself, in the lease and in a separate paper, or they do not know), and what amount does it set?
- Have they given the landlord anything in writing saying they are moving out? How did it reach the landlord (handed to the landlord or the office, regular mail, certified mail, e-mail, a resident portal request or message, a text message, or something else), and what date was it delivered?
- Are they a servicemember (including the National Guard or reserves) with military orders that affect where they live? If so, have they given the landlord a written notice of termination with a copy of the orders or a letter from the commanding officer, and what date did the landlord receive it?

### What the deadlines count from

The program computes dates only from facts the tenant has confirmed, so get these proposed and confirmed:

- The date the tenant plans to move out. The 7 days' notice count back from it.
- For a servicemember, whether the termination notice with the orders was given, and the date the landlord received it. The 30 days count from that date.

### Evidence to suggest the tenant keep

- The lease and any early termination addendum.
- The written notice of leaving, with proof of certified mail or personal delivery.
- The forwarding address given to the landlord.
- For a servicemember, the orders or the commanding officer's letter sent with the notice.
- Move-out photos and the key return date.

Tell the tenant first whether they can do each of these and what it turns on, before any step. Each condition is settled by the lease (read that clause with search_lease and say what it says), by the tenant (ask), by the program's deadlines (call get_deadlines), or not at all (the statute does not settle it: give every reading, see the open questions below). This is outside the tool: the tenant checks the military orders against the criteria in 83.682(1) (a permanent change of station of 35 miles or more, a discharge or release from active duty, orders into government quarters, temporary orders of more than 60 days to 35 miles or more away, and the others). answer:
**Short answer:** Yes, it looks like you can end your lease. Florida law lets a tenant leave when the landlord didn't give a required flood disclosure and a flood then destroys much of the tenant's belongings. Your loss is large enough to qualify. To use this right, you must give your landlord a written termination notice and move out by July 20, 2026. That date hasn't passed. Can you be fully moved out and hand back possession by July 20?

DETAILS

### Does the flood disclosure rule apply to your lease?
- Under Fla. Stat. 83.512(1), a landlord must give a prospective tenant a flood disclosure. It must be a separate document, given at or before signing a rental agreement for a term of 1 year or longer.
- Your lease runs from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026 (lease §3). That is a one-year term.
- You confirmed you were never given a flood disclosure. The lease itself has no flood disclosure in it, and the statute requires a separate document.

### Is your loss big enough?
- Section 83.512(2) calls a loss "substantial" when the "total cost of repairs to or replacement of the personal property is 50 percent or more of the personal property's market value on the date the flooding occurred."
- You told me replacement would cost about $4,000 and the items were worth about $3,000 that day. Replacement cost is well above half of the value, so your loss meets this test.

### What must you do, and by when?
- Section 83.512(2) says you may end the lease "by giving a written notice of termination and surrendering possession of the premises to the landlord no later than 30 days after the date of the damage or loss."
- The flood was June 20, 2026, so the last day is July 20, 2026. That has not passed.
- The termination takes effect only when you surrender the apartment. You need to give the written notice and move out by that date.
- Lease §6 says to leave the apartment clean and empty, return all keys to the office, and give a forwarding address in writing. Following it is a good idea.
- The statute doesn't say how to deliver the notice. Lease §7 requires written notices to the landlord to be "delivered by hand" to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or sent there by certified mail. Lease §8 says the parties did not agree to e-mail notices. Use hand delivery or certified mail, and keep proof. An e-mailed notice could be challenged.
- If you wait for a certified letter to arrive, leave enough time for it to get there before July 20.

### What happens with rent and money?
- Under §83.512(3), your landlord must refund rent or other amounts you paid in advance for any period after the termination takes effect.
- Under §83.512(4), you still owe any unpaid rent or other sums you owed before the termination date.
- This answer covers ending the lease. It doesn't cover your deposit or any claim against the landlord for your belongings. The statute section I read doesn't say the landlord must pay for your property.

### What could change this answer?
- If you can't be out by July 20, the statutory right to end the lease would likely be lost. You would then need to look at other options.
- If the landlord did give you a separate flood disclosure that you forgot about, the answer would change. You've confirmed you got none.

answer:
Yes, you very likely can end your lease. Florida law gives a tenant a way out when the landlord didn't give a required flood disclosure and the tenant then lost a lot of belongings in a flood. Your facts fit that rule. You must give written notice and hand back possession of the apartment by July 20, 2026. The termination only takes effect once you have moved out and surrendered the apartment.

Can you be fully moved out and hand the apartment back by July 20?

DETAILS

### Does the flood disclosure rule apply to you?
- Your lease runs from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2026, which is a one-year term. For a term of "1 year or longer," the landlord must give a separate flood disclosure document "at or before the execution of a rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.512(1)).
- You confirmed you never received one. The lease itself has no flood disclosure in it, and the statute requires a separate document.
- If you did get a separate flood form at signing and have forgotten it, the answer would change. You told me you did not.

### Is your loss big enough?
- The law counts a loss as "substantial" when replacement cost is "50 percent or more of the personal property's market value on the date the flooding occurred" (Fla. Stat. 83.512(2)).
- You said replacement would cost about $4,000 and the items were worth about $3,000 that day. The cost is more than the value, so it is well over 50 percent.
- Your numbers are estimates. Keep receipts, photos, and any price quotes to back them up.

### What must you do, and by when?
- The statute allows you to end the lease "by giving a written notice of termination and surrendering possession of the premises to the landlord no later than 30 days after the date of the damage or loss" (Fla. Stat. 83.512(2)).
- Counting from the June 20 flood, that last day is July 20, 2026. It has not passed.
- Termination "is effective upon the tenant surrendering possession" (Fla. Stat. 83.512(2)). A notice alone does not end the lease. You also have to move out and give the apartment back by that date.
- Your lease says written notices to the landlord must be "delivered by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, Gainesville, Florida 32608, or sent there by certified mail" (Lease §7). The statute does not say how to deliver the notice, so follow the lease. Email or the resident portal is the risky route, because the lease does not provide for it.
- Your lease also says to return all keys to the office and give a forwarding address in writing (Lease §6). Do both when you leave.
- Certified mail takes time to arrive. Hand delivery is safer for a July 20 deadline. Keep a dated copy or a receipt.

### What about rent and your deposit?
- The landlord must refund "all rent or other amounts paid in advance" for any period after the termination takes effect (Fla. Stat. 83.512(3)).
- You still owe any unpaid rent or other sums that were due before you terminated (Fla. Stat. 83.512(4)).
- The statute does not mention the security deposit. The normal deposit rules still apply to it.

### Is there a second way out?
- Florida's casualty damage law lets a tenant end the lease and leave right away if the apartment was damaged "so that the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired" and the tenant did not cause it (Fla. Stat. 83.63(1)). This depends on the condition of the apartment, not on the disclosure.
- If the apartment is still unlivable, this may also apply. You would have to show the damage substantially impaired your enjoyment of the apartment. I don't know its current condition.
- The flood disclosure route is the clearer one on your facts, because it turns on the disclosure, the numbers, and the July 20 date.
- Under Fla. Stat. 83.63(2), you must also be given a chance to collect your belongings when it is safe, or be told a date for doing so.

All three conditions must be met.

1. The tenant signed a separate addendum agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages when the lease was made: "This remedy is available only if the tenant and the landlord, at the time the rental agreement was made, indicated acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee." (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). It is met in either way:
   - The fee is written in a separate paper the tenant signed with the lease: "The tenant must indicate acceptance of liquidated damages or an early termination fee by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant can tell you. If they say the fee is written only in the lease itself, not in a separate paper, the landlord's other remedies in 83.595 apply.
   - Where the fee is written is not known yet. The tenant checks the papers signed with the lease for a separate one agreeing to the fee or liquidated damages.
2. The amount is no more than 2 months' rent: "if the amount does not exceed 2 months’ rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The tenant checks the amount the fee or liquidated damages come to, beside two months' rent.
3. For a fee, the lease asks for no more than 60 days' notice before the early termination: "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before an early termination with search_lease and say what it says. See the second open question.

The step: the notice the lease asks for, given to the landlord: "as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). If the tenant has already given a notice, ask whether it is the one the lease asks for before an early termination, in its time and way, and read that clause. Which remedy the landlord picks is open (the first open question).

### Give the landlord 7 days' written notice before leaving, by certified mail or in person, with an address, so the landlord stays held to the deposit's notice of a claim (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5))

Both conditions must be met.

1. The last day to give that notice has not passed, or the notice already went out by it: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). It is met in either way:
   - The last day has not passed. Only the program's deadlines settle this. If they show it has passed, say so.
   - The notice already given went out by the last day, by certified mail or in person, with an address. Ask the date it reached the landlord, to put beside the last day the program's deadlines show.
2. The lease does not provide otherwise on notice before moving out: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease settles this: read its clause on notice before moving out early with search_lease and say what it says.

The step: the written notice, with the address where the tenant can be reached, delivered to the landlord by certified mail or in person: "which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)).

- If the notice went by certified mail or by hand, ask the tenant to check that it gave the address where they can be reached.
- If it went by e-mail, it counts only as 83.505 allows. Ask whether the tenant and the landlord signed an addendum agreeing to notices by e-mail, and whether the notice gave the address. Read the lease's clause on notices to the landlord.
- If it went some other way, ask how it reached the landlord, beside the ways 83.49(5) names, certified mail or personal delivery.

## Deadlines

The program computes and prints every date from confirmed facts. Never write, count, or compare a date yourself: call get_deadlines, and say a deadline has passed or is upcoming only as its result says. The counting rule is an assumption: Florida's court rule for counting days has not been checked against statutory deadlines outside litigation. The program computes no date from a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.

- The tenant's 7 days' written notice before leaving. It counts back from the date the tenant plans to move out, not forward from the notice date. It goes by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached: "must give at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). If it is missed: "Failure to give such notice relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)). The lease can provide otherwise (quoted above).
- The servicemember's earliest termination date. It counts from the date the landlord received the notice, and only when the servicemember notice was given: "written notice of termination to be effective on the date stated in the notice which is at least 30 days after the landlord’s receipt of the notice" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)).

## What the statute does not settle

Each of these has no listed readings. For each, say what the tool does not work out, apply the text to what the tenant reports, and pick no answer for the law.

### Which remedy the landlord chooses

83.595 lists what the landlord may do when a tenant surrenders or abandons the unit, in four subsections: end the tenancy and the tenant's liability; relet for the tenant's account, where the landlord has "a duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)); stand by and hold the tenant liable for rent as it comes due; or charge liquidated damages or an early termination fee under a separate addendum. The choice is the landlord's. Lay the four beside what the record holds (the addendum, its amount, the monthly rent) so the tenant sees what each would mean. Never say which the landlord will choose, and never give one amount owed.

### The notice period for an early termination fee

83.595(4) refers to an early termination fee where "the tenant is required to give no more than 60 days’ notice, as provided in the rental agreement, prior to the proposed date of early termination" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)). The period comes from the lease, and the tool does not compute a date from a period the lease sets.

### Whether the servicemember criteria are met

83.682(1) applies only "if any of the following criteria are met" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(1)), and 83.682(2) says the notice "must be accompanied by either a copy of the official military orders or a written verification signed by the servicemember’s commanding officer" (Fla. Stat. 83.682(2)). Apply the criteria and the documents to what the tenant reports. A criterion the record does not show is not known yet.

### Damage to the unit

If the tenant is leaving because the unit was damaged or destroyed (for example, by fire or a storm), 83.63 may be the relevant section. There is no skill for it. Fetch it with get_statute_section before applying it, and say the tool does not compute anything for it.

## Letters

The tenant sends every letter; you send nothing. Every letter holds: today's date, the planned move-out date, the forwarding address, what the tenant asks for, and the delivery method. The postures, each line as written:

- preserve: States the planned move-out date and a forwarding address, and asks the landlord to confirm what, if anything, the landlord will charge. Cites nothing.
- assert: Adds the 83.49(5) sentence on notice before vacating, quoted.
- escalate: Adds the 83.595(4) sentence on liquidated damages or an early termination fee, quoted.

When a letter is shown, tell the tenant that the program computes the 7-day date in 83.49(5), which requires "at least 7 days’ written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating or abandoning the premises, which notice must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (Fla. Stat. 83.49(5)), counted back from the move-out date they gave. The letter is that notice only if it is sent that way and gives their new address.

The tenant delivers the letter. Read the lease's clause on where and how notices to the landlord must be sent (search_lease), and quote it when you ask how they will send it.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating what the tenant will owe as one amount. 83.595 lists the landlord's choices.
- Applying 83.595(4)'s fee or liquidated damages without the separate addendum, which the tenant must accept "by signing a separate addendum to the rental agreement" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(4)).
- Applying 83.595(2) without the landlord's "duty to exercise good faith in attempting to relet the premises" (Fla. Stat. 83.595(2)).
- Missing a way out the record points to, such as the landlord's noncompliance (through the repair skill and 83.56(1)), military orders (83.682), or damage to the unit (83.63).
- Counting the 7 days from the notice date instead of back from the move-out date.
- Computing a period the lease sets, such as the notice for an early termination fee.
- Computing any date yourself.

tool_calls.result: 83.63 Casualty damage. — If the premises are damaged or destroyed other than by the wrongful or negligent acts of the tenant so that the enjoyment of the premises is substantially impaired: (1) The tenant may terminate the rental agreement and immediately vacate the premises. The tenant may vacate the part of the premises rendered unusable by the casualty, in which case the tenant’s liability for rent shall be reduced by the fair rental value of that part of the premises damaged or destroyed. If the rental agreement is terminated, the landlord shall comply with s. 83.49 (3). (2) The tenant must be given: (a) The opportunity to collect his or her belongings from the premises when it is safe to do so; or (b) Notice of the date by which the tenant will be able to collect his or her belongings from the premises, which must occur within a reasonable time. History. — s. 2, ch. 73-330; s. 449, ch. 95-147; s. 14, ch. 2013-136; s. 1, ch. 2025-190.

tool_calls.result: 83.512 Disclosure of flood risks to prospective tenant of residential real property. — (1) A landlord must complete and provide a flood disclosure to a prospective tenant of residential real property at or before the execution of a rental agreement for a term of 1 year or longer. The flood disclosure must be in a separate document. The flood disclosure must be made in substantially the following form: FLOOD DISCLOSURE Flood Insurance: Renters’ insurance policies do not include coverage for damage resulting from floods. Tenant is encouraged to discuss the need to purchase separate flood insurance coverage with Tenant’s insurance agent. 1. Landlord has ☐ has no ☐ knowledge of any flooding that has damaged the dwelling unit during Landlord’s ownership of the dwelling unit. 2. Landlord has ☐ has not ☐ filed a claim with an insurance provider relating to flood damage in the dwelling unit, including, but not limited to, a claim with the National Flood Insurance Program. 3. Landlord has ☐ has not ☐ received assistance for flood damage to the dwelling unit, including, but not limited to, assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. 4. For the purposes of this disclosure, the term “flooding” means a general or temporary condition of partial or complete inundation of the dwelling unit caused by any of the following: a. The overflow of inland or tidal waters. b. The unusual and rapid accumulation of runoff or surface waters from any established water source, such as a river, stream, or drainage ditch. c. Sustained periods of standing water resulting from rainfall. (2) If a landlord violates this section and a tenant suffers a substantial loss or damage to the tenant’s personal property as a result of flooding, the tenant may terminate the rental agreement by giving a written notice of termination and surrendering possession of the premises to the landlord no later than 30 days after the date of the damage or loss. Termination of a rental agreement under this section is effective upon the tenant surrendering possession of the dwelling unit. For the purpose of this section, the term “substantial loss or damage” means the total cost of repairs to or replacement of the personal property is 50 percent or more of the personal property’s market value on the date the flooding occurred. (3) A landlord shall refund the tenant all rent or other amounts paid in advance under the rental agreement for any period after the effective date of the termination of the rental agreement. (4) This section does not affect a tenant’s liability for delinquent, unpaid rent or other sums owed to the landlord before the date the rental agreement was terminated by the tenant under this section. History. — s. 1, ch. 2025-166.
